system design.text: System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements.

system design interview.text: A system design interview evaluates a candidate's ability to produce technical solutions to abstract problems, so it has no single expected answer.

system design building blocks.text: The building blocks of system design are the standard components, grouped into six broad categories, that designs are assembled from.

non-functional requirements.text: A non-functional requirement specifies criteria for judging how a system operates, an overall property such as availability or performance, rather than a specific behavior.

software architecture.text: Software architecture is the set of structures needed to reason about a software system, and the discipline of creating them.

functional requirements.text: A functional requirement defines a function of a system or component as behavior between inputs and outputs, a statement of what the system is supposed to accomplish.

common scaling problems and fixes.text: Eight problems recur in large-scale production systems, and each has a standard remedy: caching, async workers, redundancy, load balancing, CDNs, object storage, central logging and database indexing or sharding.

architecture decision records.text: Architecture decision records are single, accessible records that capture each architectural decision with its technical and business justification.

software architecture activities.text: Software architecture design consists of four core activities, analysis, synthesis, evaluation and evolution, carried out iteratively.

software architecture erosion.text: Software architecture erosion is a gradual gap that opens over time between a system's intended and implemented architecture.

requirements engineering.text: Requirements engineering is the work of eliciting, analysing, specifying, validating and managing what a system must do, the 'what' that architecture answers with a 'how'.

software design pattern.text: A software design pattern is a reusable template for solving a commonly needed behavior in software, usable across programming languages and platforms.

system design interview framework.text: A system design interview goes best when worked as a fixed sequence: clarify requirements, estimate capacity, design the high-level structure, the data and the interfaces, then address scale and reliability.

requirements clarification.text: Requirements clarification is asking early about the exact scope of an interview problem and sorting what the system must do into functional, non-functional and extended requirements.

architectural patterns and styles.text: An architecture pattern is a reusable, proven solution to a recurring system-level problem, and an architecture style is a high-level structural organization of a system.

machine learning systems design.text: Machine learning systems design builds scalable, reliable and efficient systems that integrate machine learning models to solve real-world problems.

conway's law.text: Conway's law says that the structure of a system mirrors the communication structure of the organization that designs it.

discussing trade-offs in interviews.text: In the detailed design stage of an interview, present several approaches with their advantages and disadvantages, explain decisions with examples, and stay humble about what you know.

latency.text: Latency is the time delay between a cause and its effect in a system, such as the wait between sending a request and seeing the response.

bandwidth.text: In computing, bandwidth is the maximum rate of data transfer across a given path.

network latency.text: Network latency is the delay for data to cross a network, measured one-way from source to destination or as the round-trip delay time.

percentile.text: A percentile is a value that is greater than a given percentage of all the values in a sample, so the 97th percentile is above 97% of the data points.

tail latency.text: Tail latency is the high-percentile response time of a system, usually measured at the 95th, 99th or 99.9th percentile rather than as an average.

latency numbers to know.text: Rough latencies of common operations, from cache reads taking nanoseconds to a transatlantic packet taking 100 ms, let a designer judge which steps of a system are slow.

reducing latency.text: Latency is lowered with a handful of standard techniques: database indexing, load balancing, a content delivery network, async processing and data compression.

round-trip time.text: Round-trip time is the time it takes to send a signal plus the time for its acknowledgement to come back, so it includes propagation on the path between the two endpoints.

website performance metrics.text: Website performance is judged by nine metrics: load time, time to first byte, request count, DOMContentLoaded, above-the-fold load time, first contentful paint, page size, round trip time and render-blocking resources.

network throughput.text: Network throughput is the rate at which messages are successfully delivered over a communication channel.

data size units.text: Data sizes are expressed as multiples of the bit and the byte, using either decimal or binary prefixes.

latency vs throughput.text: Latency is how long one operation takes, while throughput is how many operations complete per unit of time, and one does not determine the other.

goodput.text: Goodput is the amount of useful information delivered per second to the application layer protocol.

maximum throughput measures.text: Four values describe the upper limit of what a system can deliver: maximum theoretical, asymptotic, peak measured and maximum sustained throughput.

back-of-the-envelope estimation.text: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a rough calculation built on simplified assumptions that sizes a system's users, traffic and storage before it is designed.

little's law.text: Little's law states that the long-term average number of customers in a stable system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time a customer spends in the system.

osi model.text: The OSI model is a logical, conceptual model that splits network communication into seven abstract layers, each stacked on the last.

tcp/ip model.text: The TCP/IP model, also called the Internet protocol suite, organizes the Internet's protocols into four layers (link, internet, transport and application) according to each protocol's scope.

client-server model.text: The client-server model splits the work of a distributed application between servers, which provide a resource or service, and clients, which request it.

osi model layers.text: The OSI model has seven layers; from top to bottom they are application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link and physical.

transmission control protocol.text: TCP is one of the main Internet protocols, providing reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes between applications on hosts communicating over an IP network.

transport layer.text: The transport layer carries variable-length data sequences from an application on a source host to an application on a destination host across a network.

encapsulation and de-encapsulation.text: Encapsulation is the nesting of a data payload inside a packet with a header, which each layer of the network stack does in turn as data is sent.

internet protocol.text: The Internet Protocol (IP) is the network-layer protocol that relays datagrams across network boundaries.

tcp connection setup and teardown.text: TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake and closes it with a four-way handshake in which each side stops its own half independently.

application-layer protocols.text: Network protocols are standard methods of transferring data between two computers in a network.

ip address.text: An IP address is a numerical label assigned to a device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol, so that the device can be found and addressed.

user datagram protocol.text: UDP is a core Internet protocol that sends messages, carried as datagrams in packets, to other hosts on an IP network.

port numbers.text: A port number identifies a service on a host, which lets many connections share one IP address.

network socket.text: A network socket is a software endpoint in a network node for sending and receiving data across a network, identified externally by its protocol, IP address and port number.

ipv4 versus ipv6.text: IPv6 replaces IPv4's 32-bit addresses with 128-bit addresses, driven by the need for more internet addresses and simpler network management.

tcp versus udp.text: TCP is a connection-oriented, reliable, ordered protocol, while UDP is a simpler, connectionless, message-based protocol with no delivery guarantees.

udp use cases.text: UDP suits applications that value low latency over perfect delivery, such as voice, video, games and simple query-response lookups.

best-effort delivery.text: IP provides only best-effort delivery: it is connectionless and unreliable, and the end hosts and upper-layer protocols must repair any faults.

tcp reliable delivery.text: TCP numbers every byte, and the receiver acknowledges what it has received so the sender can detect lost data and retransmit it.

tcp flow control.text: Flow control keeps a TCP sender from sending data faster than the receiver can receive and process it reliably.

ip addressing methods.text: IP has four principal addressing methods, unicast, broadcast, multicast and anycast, which differ in how many receivers a message reaches.

mtu and ip fragmentation.text: The maximum transmission unit (MTU) is the largest packet a link can carry, and IPv4 fragments any datagram that exceeds it.

tcp congestion control.text: TCP congestion control is the set of sender-side mechanisms (a congestion window, slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery) that keep a connection from sending more than the network can carry.

address resolution protocol.text: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) discovers the link-layer address, such as a MAC address, that goes with an internet-layer address, typically an IPv4 address.

head-of-line blocking.text: Head-of-line blocking is the delay that occurs when data that arrived later cannot be used until earlier lost or reordered data has been retransmitted and received.

quic.text: QUIC is a general-purpose transport protocol normally layered on UDP that multiplexes streams over a connection and builds TLS into its handshake, designed to replace TCP for many applications.

network address translation.text: Network address translation (NAT) maps one IP address space into another by rewriting address information in packet headers as they cross a routing device, so a whole private network can share one public address.

public and private ip addresses.text: A public IP address is globally routable and used between hosts on the Internet, while a private address is reserved for use inside a private network.

static and dynamic ip addresses.text: A static IP address is configured persistently and does not change, while a dynamic IP address is assigned by the network each time a host joins or restarts.

dynamic host configuration protocol.text: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically assigns IP addresses and other communication parameters to devices on a network, using a client-server architecture.

dhcp lease process.text: A DHCP client obtains an IP address through four exchanges (discovery, offer, request and acknowledgement) and then holds it as a lease that it must renew.

subnets and cidr notation.text: A subnet is a part of an IP network; an address is split into a network prefix and a host part, and CIDR notation states where the split falls.

tcp retransmission timeout.text: The retransmission timeout (RTO) is how long a TCP sender waits for an acknowledgment before resending a segment, and it must be determined dynamically.

tcp segmentation and mss.text: Segmentation is how TCP cuts an application's byte stream into segments, and the Maximum Segment Size option tells the peer the largest segment it will accept.

tcp sequence numbers.text: TCP gives every octet of data on a connection a sequence number, which lets the receiver acknowledge, order and de-duplicate what it receives.

nagle's algorithm.text: Nagle's algorithm makes TCP wait for a full packet of data before sending, grouping small messages into a single packet.

tcp three-way handshake.text: The three-way handshake is the procedure TCP uses to establish a connection, in which the two peers exchange and acknowledge each other's initial sequence numbers.

tcp connection states.text: A TCP connection moves through a fixed set of states during its life, changing state in response to user calls, incoming segments and timeouts.

selective acknowledgment.text: Selective acknowledgment (SACK) is a TCP option that lets the receiver acknowledge discontinuous blocks of correctly received data, so the sender resends only what is missing.

internet control message protocol.text: The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is a supporting protocol that routers and other network devices use to send error messages and operational information about IP communication.

choosing between tcp and udp.text: Use TCP when data must arrive complete and in order, and use UDP when the lowest latency matters more than losing some data.

syn flood and other tcp attacks.term: SYN flood and other TCP attacks
syn flood and other tcp attacks.text: TCP can be attacked in several ways, including denial of service by SYN flood and connection hijacking.

network layer.text: The network layer transfers packets from one node to another across different networks, finding a route through intermediate nodes where needed.

nat traversal.text: NAT traversal is the set of techniques, such as port forwarding and TCP hole punching, that let peers behind different NATs communicate with each other.

delayed acknowledgment.text: A delayed ACK means a receiver sends fewer than one acknowledgment per data segment received, which saves effort in both the network and the hosts.

silly window syndrome.text: Silly window syndrome is a stable pattern of small incremental window movements that leaves TCP performing extremely poorly.

tcp half-close.text: Because TCP closes the two directions of a connection independently, an endpoint can stop sending while it keeps receiving.

tcp keep-alive.text: A TCP keep-alive sends a probe on an idle connection to check that the peer is still there.

tcp reset.text: A reset (RST) segment tells a TCP peer that a segment does not belong to a live connection, so the receiver ignores it or aborts the connection.

tcp segment header.text: A TCP header follows the IP header and carries the fields TCP needs: ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, flags, window and checksum.

time-wait state.text: TIME-WAIT is the state in which the endpoint that closed a TCP connection first lingers, so that late segments from the old connection cannot disturb a new one.

domain name system.text: A hierarchical, distributed naming service that translates human-readable domain names into the numeric IP addresses that computers use to find each other.

zero-window probing.text: Zero-window probing is how a TCP sender keeps testing a receiver whose window is zero, so that the reopening of the window is reliably reported.

path mtu discovery.text: Path MTU Discovery is a technique for finding the smallest MTU along the route between two IP hosts, so packets can be sized to avoid fragmentation.

tcp congestion control algorithms.text: TCP congestion control algorithms are variants of the window-adjustment rules, such as Reno, CUBIC and BBR, that differ in how they detect and react to congestion.

anycast.text: Anycast is an addressing and routing method in which one IP address is shared by servers in many locations, and traffic goes to the nearest one.

dns transport protocols.text: DNS queries travel over classic UDP and TCP on port 53 or over encrypted transports such as DNS over TLS, DNS over HTTPS, DNS over QUIC and DNSCrypt.

domain name hierarchy.text: The DNS namespace is a tree whose nodes each have a label, and a full domain name is the labels from a node up to the root, joined by dots.

top-level domain.text: A top-level domain is the highest level of the DNS hierarchy below the root, the last label of any domain name, such as .com in www.example.com.

time to live and hop limit.term: Time to live and hop limit
time to live and hop limit.text: Time to live (TTL), or hop limit, is a mechanism that limits the lifespan of data in a computer or network.

dns resource records.text: Resource records are the information elements of the DNS database, each with a type, a time to live, a class and type-specific data.

dns record types.text: The record types of DNS name the kinds of information a domain publishes, such as addresses (A, AAAA), aliases (CNAME), mail servers (MX), name servers (NS), reverse pointers (PTR), services (SRV) and text (TXT).

domain name registration.text: The right to use a domain name is delegated by registrars, which are accredited by ICANN or similar organizations, while a registry runs the database of names for each TLD.

hosts.txt and dns origins.text: DNS replaced the single centrally maintained HOSTS.TXT file of ARPANET host names, which became slow and unwieldy as the network grew.

specialized dns record types.text: Beyond A, AAAA, MX and NS, DNS defines many more record types for aliases, service discovery, certificates, DNSSEC and zone transfers.

reverse dns lookup.text: A reverse DNS lookup queries the DNS for the domain names tied to an IP address that is already known.

cname records and aliases.text: A CNAME record marks its owner name as an alias and names the canonical (primary) name that holds the real data.

dns components.text: DNS has three major components: the domain name space with its resource records, name servers that hold the data, and resolvers that extract it for clients.

dns design goals.text: DNS was designed to give one consistent name space that is distributed and cached, useful for many applications, and independent of any one network, protocol or host type.

domain name registrar.text: A domain name registrar is a company or office, accredited by a registry, that manages the reservation of Internet domain names for registrants.

dns lookup process.text: To resolve a name, a resolver asks a root server, then a top-level domain server, then the domain's authoritative server, following referrals until it receives an authoritative answer.

dns resolver.text: The client side of DNS, which initiates and sequences the queries that end in a full resolution, such as turning a domain name into an IP address.

subdomain.text: A subdomain is an extra part added to a main domain name, commonly used to split a website into logical sections.

dns caching and ttl.text: DNS reduces query load by caching resolution results locally or on intermediary resolvers, each result carrying a time to live (TTL) that says how long it stays valid.

dns load distribution.text: DNS can spread traffic and add fault tolerance because hostnames and IP addresses need not match one to one: one name can resolve to many addresses and different users can get different answers.

dns security issues.text: DNS was designed without strong security, so responses can be forged or abused, and extensions such as DNSSEC and TSIG were added to authenticate them.

recursive and iterative queries.text: Resolvers are classified by query method: in a recursive query a server resolves the name fully on the client's behalf, in an iterative query the client follows referrals, and a non-recursive query needs no further rounds.

dnssec.text: DNSSEC is a suite of IETF extensions that secures DNS data by adding digital signatures, so resolvers can detect forged or altered answers.

round-robin dns.text: Round-robin DNS spreads load across several servers by answering a name lookup with a list of IP addresses whose order is rotated on each response.

dns cache poisoning.text: DNS cache poisoning, also called DNS spoofing, introduces corrupt data into a resolver's cache so that it returns a wrong answer, such as an attacker's IP address.

root and tld name servers.text: Root name servers direct resolvers to the right top-level domain servers, and TLD name servers hold the information for every domain under one extension such as .com.

authoritative name server.text: A name server that answers DNS queries only from data configured by an original source, such as the domain administrator, rather than from a cache of another server's answers.

dns privacy.text: Because DNS has no confidentiality controls, queries are exposed, and the ways of protecting them are themselves argued over.

stub resolver.text: A stub resolver moves the resolution work off the local machine and into a name server that supports recursive queries, keeping only a list of such servers.

dns delegation.text: Delegation is the mechanism that assigns responsibility for different parts of the DNS namespace to different name servers.

dns zone.text: A zone is a connected region of the name space, bounded by cuts where authority is handed on, for which a set of name servers holds the authoritative data.

dns zone transfer.text: A zone transfer is how a secondary name server polls its primary and copies a changed zone, so every authoritative server for a zone serves the same data.

dns availability over consistency.text: DNS favors availability of name data over instant consistency: updates spread gradually, and cached copies expire on timers that the data's owner sets.

dnssec chain of trust.text: DNSSEC validation follows a chain of linked DS and DNSKEY records from a trust anchor, usually the DNS root key, down to the zone that signed the answer.

dnssec denial of existence.text: DNSSEC proves that a name does not exist by returning signed NSEC or NSEC3 records that show where a gap in the zone lies.

dnssec key management.text: DNSSEC key management covers the key signing and zone signing keys, how they are rolled over, and how signature validity is limited in time.

split-horizon dns.text: Split-horizon DNS lets a DNS implementation return different sets of DNS information for the same query, usually chosen by the source address of the request.

dns message format.text: DNS queries and responses share one message format: a header followed by question, answer, authority and additional sections.

dns standard queries.text: A standard query names a domain (QNAME), a record type (QTYPE) and a class (QCLASS) and asks a name server for the matching records.

dns resolver algorithm.text: RFC 1034's resolver algorithm answers from local data if it can and otherwise finds the best servers, queries them and analyzes each response.

http.text: HTTP is a stateless, application-layer request-response protocol that clients and servers use to exchange hypertext and other content, and it is the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web.

public-key cryptography.text: Public-key cryptography, or asymmetric cryptography, uses pairs of related keys, a public key that can be shared openly and a private key that must stay secret.

http request and response messages.text: An HTTP message is a header followed by an optional body; clients send request messages and servers answer with response messages.

http persistent connections.text: A persistent connection lets one TCP connection be reused for more than one HTTP request and response.

http request methods.text: The request method, informally a verb, is the primary source of request semantics: it names the action the client wants applied to the target resource.

http statelessness and sessions.text: HTTP is stateless, so the meaning of each request can be understood in isolation, and a web application that must remember a user across requests builds its own session on top.

http cookie.text: An HTTP cookie is a small block of data that a web server creates and the user's browser stores and sends back, giving stateless HTTP a memory of earlier requests.

http status codes.text: An HTTP status code is a three-digit number in a response that describes the result of the request and the semantics of the response.

idempotent http methods.text: A request method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of several identical requests with it is the same as the effect of a single such request.

safe http methods.text: A request method is safe if its defined semantics are essentially read-only: the client does not request or expect any state change on the origin server.

digital certificates and certificate aut.text: A digital certificate certifies that a named subject owns a public key, and certificate authorities are trusted third parties that sign certificates so others can rely on them.

symmetric-key encryption.text: Symmetric-key encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt plaintext and to decrypt ciphertext, so both parties must hold that shared secret.

diffie-hellman key exchange.text: Diffie-Hellman key exchange is a mathematical method of securely generating a shared symmetric key over a public channel.

certificate chain of trust.text: A chain of trust lets a certificate be validated against its parent certificates, back to a root certificate that serves as a trust anchor.

certificate authority trust risks.text: A certificate authority is a trusted third party that stores, signs and issues digital certificates, so the whole system's security depends on it.

rsa cryptosystem.text: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem in which publicly revealing the encryption key does not reveal the decryption key, so anyone can encrypt for the key's owner and the owner can sign messages.

http client error status codes.text: The 4xx class says the client seems to have erred; the server should explain the error and whether it is temporary or permanent, and the codes apply to any method.

http authentication.text: HTTP provides a general framework for access control, with extensible challenge-response schemes the server uses to challenge a request and the client uses to supply credentials.

http intermediaries.text: An HTTP intermediary is a proxy, gateway or tunnel placed between client and origin server so a request can be satisfied through a chain of connections.

http redirection status codes.text: The 3xx class says the user agent must take further action to fulfill the request, usually by repeating it at a different URI.

http server error status codes.text: The 5xx class says the server is aware it has erred or cannot perform the requested method.

http caching.text: An HTTP cache is a local store of earlier responses, with the subsystem that controls their storage, retrieval and deletion, which reuses a prior response to answer a later request and so improves performance.

http cache freshness.text: A cached response is fresh while its age has not exceeded its freshness lifetime, and a fresh response can be reused without contacting the origin server.

additional http status codes.text: RFC 6585 defines four optional HTTP status codes, 428, 429, 431 and 511, for common situations that less precise codes handled poorly.

http versions.text: HTTP has evolved through versions 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3, each changing how requests share connections and which transport carries them.

http/2.text: HTTP/2 is a revision of HTTP that maps HTTP semantics onto binary frames multiplexed over one connection, for lower latency and more efficient use of the network than HTTP/1.1.

certificate revocation.text: A certificate can be revoked before it expires, for example because its private key was compromised, and browsers check whether that has happened.

http/3 and quic.text: HTTP/3 is the third major version of HTTP, which runs over QUIC, a multiplexed transport built on UDP, instead of over TCP.

http/2 streams and multiplexing.text: An HTTP/2 stream is an independent, bidirectional sequence of frames within one connection, and giving each request and response its own stream is how HTTP/2 multiplexes requests.

http pipelining.text: HTTP pipelining is a feature of HTTP/1.1 that lets a client send several HTTP requests over one TCP connection without waiting for the matching responses.

certificate validation levels.text: Validation levels describe how much a certificate authority checks before issuing a certificate: domain control only, organization identity, or extended legal identity.

non-standard http status codes.text: Non-standard status codes are values that web servers, proxies and platforms use although no IETF standard defines them.

http extensibility.text: HTTP has generic extension points, such as methods, status codes, header fields, authentication schemes and cache directives, that add capabilities without a new protocol version.

http informational status codes.text: A 1xx status code is an interim response that reports connection status or request progress before the final response.

http resources and representations.text: A resource is the target of an HTTP request, and a representation is information reflecting the past, current or desired state of a resource in a format the protocol can carry.

http content negotiation.text: Content negotiation is how HTTP chooses among several representations of a resource, such as different formats, languages or encodings, to fit what a client can handle or prefers.

http content type, encoding and length.term: HTTP content type, encoding and length
http content type, encoding and length.text: Representation metadata describes the content of a message: Content-Type gives its media type, Content-Encoding the codings applied, such as compression, and Content-Length its size in octets.

http success status codes.text: The 2xx class says the client's request was successfully received, understood and accepted.

http/2 connection management.text: HTTP/2 uses one long-lived, persistent connection per host and port, reused across requests and shut down gracefully with a GOAWAY frame.

http/2 flow control.text: HTTP/2 flow control is a credit-based scheme, driven by the receiver, that keeps multiplexed streams on one connection from destructively interfering with each other.

http/2 header compression.text: HTTP/2 compresses each set of header fields into a field block (HPACK) using state shared across the connection, which shrinks the repetitive headers HTTP carries.

http/2 server push.text: HTTP/2 server push lets a server send responses, with the promised requests that go with them, to a client before the client asks for them.

keeping sensitive data out of urls.term: Keeping sensitive data out of URLs
keeping sensitive data out of urls.text: URIs are meant to be shared, not secured, so sensitive or personally identifiable information should not be placed in them.

post versus put.text: POST hands the enclosed representation to the resource to process by its own semantics, while PUT replaces the target resource's state with it.

vary header.text: The Vary response header names the request fields, beyond method and URI, that may have influenced which content the origin server chose.

cache-control header.text: The Cache-Control header lists directives that control caches along the request and response chain.

transport layer security.text: TLS is a cryptographic protocol that provides secured communications over a computer network, giving applications privacy, integrity and authenticity.

cache-control request directives.text: Request directives let a client suggest how a cache should treat a request, but they are advisory and caches need not honor them.

shared and private http caches.text: A shared cache stores responses for reuse by more than one user and sits usually in an intermediary, while a private cache is dedicated to one user, often inside a user agent.

http cache security risks.text: Caches add an attack surface, because their contents persist after a request ends and an attack on a cache can reveal or alter information long afterwards.

https.text: HTTPS is HTTP carried over an encrypted TLS connection, so web traffic is private, authenticated and protected from tampering in transit.

man-in-the-middle attack.text: A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack, or on-path attack, is one where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are talking directly.

securing cookies.text: Securing cookies means protecting the session identifiers that cookies carry from theft and misuse, using encryption, cookie attributes and input filtering.

datagram transport layer security.text: Datagram TLS (DTLS) is a protocol based on TLS that secures datagram-based applications against eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery.

http strict transport security.text: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) lets a website tell browsers to use only HTTPS connections to it, protecting against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrades and cookie hijacking.

forward secrecy.text: Forward secrecy is a property of a cryptographic system that keeps a session key safe even if one of the private keys is compromised in the future.

http origins and certificate verificatio.text: An origin is the scheme, host and port of a URI, and for https URIs a client must verify that the server's certificate matches that origin before trusting the connection.

secure sockets layer.text: SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, is a protocol for encrypting and securing communications on the internet, now deprecated in favor of TLS.

tls handshake.text: In the TLS handshake the client and server agree on cipher parameters, the server proves its identity with a certificate, and both derive a shared session key for the secured connection.

tls versions.text: TLS has gone through versions 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, each defined in an RFC and each revised to address security threats.

server name indication.text: Server Name Indication is a TLS extension in which the client names the host it wants in its ClientHello, so a server hosting several sites can send the right certificate.

tls 1.3.text: TLS 1.3 is the current version of Transport Layer Security, designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery between client and server applications.

tls cipher suites and key exchange.term: TLS cipher suites and key exchange
tls cipher suites and key exchange.text: Before sending protected data, a TLS client and server must agree on an encryption key and a cipher, choosing among several key exchange, cipher and integrity methods.

tls interception.text: TLS interception is decrypting, reading and re-encrypting an encrypted data stream in transit, usually through a transparent proxy.

limits of https protection.text: HTTPS protects content in transit but leaves some information visible and depends on correct implementation and on clients actually using it.

starting an http/2 connection.text: An HTTP/2 connection starts with TLS and the ALPN extension for https URIs, or with prior knowledge for cleartext http, and each side then sends a connection preface.

mutual tls.text: Mutual TLS, or mTLS, is a method of mutual authentication in which both ends of a connection verify that the other holds the correct private key.

types of tls certificate.text: TLS certificates come in several types by what they identify: servers, clients, several names at once, or whole families of subdomains.

symmetric session keys in https.text: HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption only to set up a session key and then switches to symmetric encryption for the data.

tls session resumption.text: A resumed TLS session reuses the results of an earlier handshake, through a session ID, a session ticket or, in TLS 1.3, a pre-shared key, so the handshake can skip expensive public-key operations.

tls 0-rtt early data.text: TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT) lets a client that shares a pre-shared key with the server send application data in its first flight, saving a round trip at the cost of weaker security.

http conditional requests.text: A conditional request carries header fields that set a precondition to be tested before the method is applied to the target resource.

http cache validation.text: Validation, or revalidation, is a cache using a conditional request to ask the next server whether a stored response is still valid instead of fetching it in full.

http range requests.text: A range request asks for only part of a representation, such as the remainder of an interrupted download, by sending a Range header on a GET.

http validators and entity tags.text: A validator is resource metadata that can be used in a precondition to make a conditional request; HTTP defines modification dates and opaque entity tags.

cache-control response directives.text: Response directives are instructions from the origin server that tell caches whether and for how long a response may be stored and reused.

http cache invalidation.text: Invalidation is a cache removing or marking invalid its stored responses for a URI, so a mandatory validation is needed before any is used again.

storing and reusing http cached response.term: Storing and reusing HTTP cached responses
storing and reusing http cached response.text: A cache may store a response only if it passes storage checks and may reuse a stored response only if the new request matches it and the response is fresh, allowed stale or validated.

hash function.text: A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, called hash values, hash codes, digests or hashes, which are usually used to index a hash table.

base64.text: Base64 is a binary-to-text encoding that represents each 6-bit segment of the data with one of 64 printable characters, so binary data can travel over channels that carry only text.

hash collision.text: A hash collision happens when two distinct pieces of data share the same hash value.

birthday attack.text: A birthday attack finds any two inputs that collide, which is easier than finding one that matches a specific value.

open addressing.text: A way to handle collisions in which, on a collision, the table is probed for an alternate empty cell.

separate chaining.text: A way to handle collisions in which records that hash to the same cell go into a linked list in that cell.

bloom filter.text: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is a member of a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives.

false positive.text: A Bloom filter answer that says an element is in the set because other elements set its bits by chance.

quadtree.text: A tree data structure in which each internal node has exactly four children, used to partition two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants.

md5.text: MD5 is a widely used hash function that produces a 128-bit hash value, typically written as 32 hexadecimal digits.

k-d tree.text: A k-d tree is a space-partitioning data structure, a binary tree whose nodes are points, for organizing points in a k-dimensional space.

trie.text: A trie, also called a prefix tree or digital tree, is a search tree for storing and retrieving strings from a dictionary or set.

radix tree.text: A radix tree, or compressed trie, merges any node that has only one child into its parent.

z-order curve.text: The Z-order, or Morton, curve maps multidimensional data to one dimension while preserving locality: points close together in several dimensions usually lie close together in the order.

geohash.text: A geocoding method that encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.

distributed unique id generation.text: A distributed unique ID generator produces globally unique numerical IDs that are roughly sorted by time and generated at low latency by many machines.

hilbert curve.text: The Hilbert curve is a continuous space-filling fractal curve, first described by David Hilbert in 1891, that maps between one and two dimensions while preserving locality fairly well.

similarity hashing.text: Similarity hashing, or fuzzy hashing, produces hashes that show when data is similar but not identical.

perceptual hash.text: A fingerprint of multimedia that is a type of locality-sensitive hash, so similar features give similar hashes.

string hashing.text: String hashing folds the characters of a variable-length string into a fixed-size hash code.

universally unique identifier.text: A 128-bit number used to identify information in computer systems, generated without any central authority.

snowflake id.text: A form of unique identifier used in distributed computing that packs a timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence number into one number.

uuid versions.text: The UUID versions are the ways of filling a UUID's bits: time and node based, name hash based, random, time-ordered with random bits, or custom.

uuid best practices.text: RFC 9562 advises how to generate, store, sort and protect UUIDs so that they stay unique, sortable and safe to use in databases and distributed systems.

security capability.text: An identifier whose mere possession grants access.

count-min sketch.text: A count-min sketch is a probabilistic data structure that serves as a frequency table of events in a stream of data.

merkle tree.text: A Merkle tree, or hash tree, is a tree in which each leaf is labelled with the cryptographic hash of a data block and each inner node with the hash of its children's labels.

hyperloglog.text: An algorithm for the count-distinct problem that approximates the number of distinct elements in a multiset using very little memory.

cache filtering with a bloom filter.term: Cache filtering with a Bloom filter
cache filtering with a bloom filter.text: Using a Bloom filter to remember which URLs were requested so a web cache stores an object only when it is requested a second time.

counting bloom filter.text: A Bloom filter variant whose array positions are counters instead of single bits, which lets it delete elements.

bloom filter alternatives.text: Set-membership filters such as cuckoo, quotient and xor filters that store short fingerprints of keys and can beat the classic Bloom filter on space, speed or deletion.

quadtree types.text: Quadtrees are classified by the kind of data they hold, such as areas, points, lines and curves, and by whether the tree's shape depends on the order data is added.

limits of geohash proximity search.text: Using shared geohash prefixes to find nearby points works for most points but fails near cell borders, the poles and the 180 degree meridian.

nearby search with a quadtree.text: A way to find nearby businesses by building an in-memory quadtree of all locations and walking it down to the leaf that holds the search origin.

load balancing.text: Load balancing distributes a set of tasks or incoming network traffic across several computing resources, sending requests only to those that are online, so the overall work is processed more efficiently.

dns load balancing.text: DNS load balancing configures a domain in the Domain Name System so that client requests to it are spread across a group of servers.

load balancing algorithms.text: Scheduling algorithms, also called load-balancing methods, are the rules a load balancer uses to decide which back-end server receives each request.

power of two choices.text: A method that picks two servers at random and chooses the better of the two.

session persistence.text: Session persistence, also called stickiness, sends all requests in one user session to the same backend server so that session data kept there can be found.

static and dynamic load balancing.text: A load-balancing algorithm is static when it ignores the current state of the system and dynamic when it takes each node's current load into account.

client-side load balancing.text: In client-side random load balancing, the client receives a list of server IPs and picks one at random for each connection.

master-worker load balancing.text: In a master-worker scheme, a master hands out tasks to workers that ask for them, making it one of the simplest dynamic load balancing algorithms.

round robin load balancing.text: Round robin sends each new request to the next server in sequence and starts again at the first server after the last.

session state storage.text: Session state can be kept in a database, in the client's browser, or in a distributed hash table, so that the balancer is free to pick any backend server.

work stealing.text: Work stealing gives each processor some tasks, then lets idle processors take work from busy or overloaded ones.

layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing.text: A layer 4 load balancer routes on transport-level information such as IP addresses and ports, while a layer 7 load balancer reads whole requests and routes on their content.

hardware, software and cloud load balanc.term: Hardware, software and cloud load balancers
hardware, software and cloud load balanc.text: Load balancers come as physical hardware devices, as software on standard machines, or as managed cloud services.

global server load balancing.text: Global server load balancing distributes traffic across multiple geographical locations to improve redundancy and performance at a global scale.

health checks.text: A health check lets the load balancer tell whether a server is down or performing poorly so it can remove that server from the pool.

load balancer failover.text: Load balancing is often used to implement failover, the continuation of service after the failure of one or more components.

n+1.text: At least one component in excess of the service's capacity.

load balancer features.text: Beyond distributing requests, load balancers offer a range of extra features, most of them vendor specific, such as compression, caching, security and connection handling.

connection multiplexing.text: Consolidating multiple HTTP requests from multiple clients into a single TCP socket to the backends.

tls termination.text: A load balancer or reverse proxy can terminate TLS connections itself, decrypting traffic and passing plain requests to the backend servers so they are spared the encryption work.

proxy server.text: A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it: the client sends the request to the proxy, which evaluates it and performs the required network transactions.

forward proxy.text: A forward proxy is a server that sits in front of a group of client machines and communicates with Internet servers on their behalf.

reverse proxy.text: A reverse proxy, or surrogate server, is a proxy server that appears to clients to be an ordinary web server but merely forwards their requests to one or more ordinary web servers.

api gateway.text: An API gateway is an API management tool that sits between clients and a set of backend services as their single entry point, enforcing security and throttling policies before passing requests on.

haproxy.text: HAProxy is free, open source software that provides a high-availability load balancer and proxy for TCP and HTTP-based applications, spreading requests across multiple servers.

caching proxy.text: A caching proxy speeds up requests by returning content saved from an earlier request by the same or another client.

nginx.text: nginx is a web server that can also be used as a reverse proxy, load balancer, mail proxy and HTTP cache.

transparent proxy.text: A transparent or intercepting proxy redirects or filters client traffic without being explicitly selected by the client.

reverse proxy trade-offs.text: Putting a reverse proxy in front of servers adds complexity and creates a single point of failure and a high-value security target.

api gateway request flow.text: An API gateway handles each request in stages: it validates the request, checks identity and rate limits, routes it to a service and deals with errors.

caching.text: A cache is a hardware or software component that stores data, either a copy of data kept elsewhere or the result of an earlier computation, so that future requests for it can be served faster.

reverse proxy vs api gateway vs load bal.term: Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer
reverse proxy vs api gateway vs load bal.text: A reverse proxy, an API gateway and a load balancer are three components that sit in front of servers, each suited to a different job (hiding and protecting servers, routing to services, spreading traffic), and a system can use all three together.

backend for frontend pattern.text: The Backend For Frontend pattern creates a separate backend service for each specific frontend application or interface.

api management.text: API management is the process of publishing web APIs, enforcing their usage policies, controlling access, supporting their users, and collecting and analyzing usage statistics and performance.

locality of reference.text: Locality of reference is the tendency of a processor or application to access the same set of memory locations, or nearby ones, repeatedly over a short period.

cache hit ratio.text: The hit ratio of a cache is how often a searched-for item is found in it, expressed as the percentage of accesses that are cache hits.

cpu cache.text: A CPU cache is a hardware cache used by the processor to reduce the average time or energy needed to access data from main memory.

cache eviction policies.text: Cache replacement policies, also called eviction policies, are algorithms that decide which items a full cache discards to make room for new data.

cache write policies.text: A cache's write policy governs when a write made to the cache is propagated to the backing store, and a write-miss policy governs whether data is loaded into the cache on a write miss.

least frequently used.text: Least frequently used (LFU) counts how often each item is needed and discards the items used less often first.

least recently used.text: Least recently used (LRU) is an eviction policy that discards the least recently used items first.

cache coherence.text: Cache coherence is the uniformity of shared resource data that is stored in multiple local caches.

page cache.text: A page cache, or disk cache, is a transparent cache in main memory for pages that originate from a secondary storage device such as a hard disk or SSD.

caching strategies.text: Caching strategies are the patterns for keeping a cache and its database in sync: cache-aside and read-through for reads, and write-around, write-back and write-through for writes.

distributed cache.text: A distributed cache pools the RAM of multiple networked computers into a single in-memory data store used as a data cache to provide fast access to data.

buffer versus cache.text: A cache reduces accesses to slower underlying storage for data transferred repeatedly, while a buffer reduces the number of transfers of otherwise novel data between communicating processes.

cache prefetching.text: Prefetching loads data into a cache ahead of time, guessing that the next chunk or two of data will soon be required.

redis.text: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory key-value database used as a distributed cache and message broker, with optional durability.

memcached.text: Memcached is a general-purpose distributed memory-caching system, often used to speed up dynamic database-driven websites by caching data and objects in RAM so an external data source is read less often.

redis replication and clustering.text: Redis scales reads and protects data through master-replica replication, and scales further through a clustering mode.

memoization.text: Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up programs by storing the results of expensive function calls and returning them when the same inputs occur again.

belady's optimal algorithm.text: Bélády's optimal algorithm, also called the optimal replacement policy or the clairvoyant algorithm, discards the information that will not be needed for the longest time.

fifo and random eviction.text: Simple eviction policies choose the victim without tracking recency or frequency: FIFO evicts the oldest entry, LIFO the newest, and random replacement an arbitrary one.

most recently used.text: Most recently used (MRU) is the reverse of LRU: it discards the most recently used items first.

sieve and s3-fifo.text: SIEVE is a simple eviction algorithm designed specifically for web caches such as key-value caches and content delivery networks.

segmented lru.text: A segmented LRU (SLRU) cache is divided into a probationary segment and a protected segment.

adaptive replacement cache.text: The adaptive replacement cache (ARC) is a page replacement algorithm that outperforms LRU by tracking both frequently used and recently used pages plus a recent eviction history for both.

caching layers.text: Data is cached at many layers of a system, from the client-facing side to backend systems.

time to live.text: Time to live (TTL) gives each cache item a specific lifespan after which it is dropped or refreshed.

cache invalidation.text: Cache invalidation is the process by which a computer system declares cache entries out of date and replaces or removes them.

cache-aside.text: In cache-aside the application reads from the cache first and, on a miss, reads the data from the database and then updates the cache.

cache stampede.text: A cache stampede, also called dog-piling, is a cascading failure in which very heavy load makes many parallel processes recompute the same expired cached value at once.

cache stampede mitigation.text: Cache stampede mitigation, also called dogpile prevention, covers techniques that stop many processes from recomputing one expired cache value at the same moment.

cache penetration.text: Cache penetration happens when the requested key exists in neither the cache nor the database, so every such request ends up at the database.

cache failure modes.text: Caches typically go wrong in four ways: many keys expiring together, requests for keys that do not exist, a hot key expiring, and the cache crashing.

multi-level caching.text: Multi-level caching keeps data in a hierarchy of cache levels, labeled L1, L2, L3 and so on, with each level searched in turn.

redis persistence.text: Redis persists its in-memory dataset to disk either by snapshotting at intervals or by journaling every change to an append-only file.

choosing between memcached and redis.text: Redis and Memcached are both used as caches, and the choice between them is a popular interview question that turns on the data structures, persistence and scaling each offers.

cache purge, refresh and ban.text: Purge, refresh and ban are three methods of explicitly invalidating content held in a caching proxy.

thundering herd problem.text: The thundering herd problem occurs when many processes or threads are awakened at once but only one can use the resource, so the rest fail and go back to sleep.

content delivery network.text: A geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them.

peer-to-peer.text: Peer-to-peer (P2P) is a distributed architecture in which participants share part of their own resources, such as processing power, storage or network capacity, directly with other peers.

ddos.text: A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack makes a machine or network resource unavailable by flooding it with traffic that comes from many different sources.

cdn origin and edge servers.text: The origin server holds the original content, and edge servers are the many caching servers spread around the world that serve users nearby.

image cdn.text: An Image CDN serves multiple versions of the same image over HTTP depending on the properties of the requesting browser.

peer-to-peer cdn.text: A peer-to-peer CDN is one in which clients provide resources as well as use them.

cdn request flow.text: A user's request is answered from the nearest edge server's cache, or the edge fetches the content from the origin, stores a copy and delivers it.

private cdn.text: A private CDN is a content delivery network built by a content owner, made of PoPs that serve content only for that owner.

telco cdn.text: A telco CDN is a content delivery network launched by a telecommunications service provider on the network it owns.

virtual cdn.text: A virtual CDN, also called a software-defined CDN, uses virtualization to deploy CDN caches dynamically.

push and pull cdns.text: CDNs are divided into push CDNs, which are sent new content whenever it changes, and pull CDNs, which fetch content from the origin when a user first requests it.

cdn request routing.text: Request routing directs each client request to the content source best able to serve it, such as the closest node or the one with the most capacity.

content networking techniques.text: A CDN is an intelligent overlay on the Internet's simple core network that combines web caching, server-load balancing, request routing and content services.

edge content service protocols.text: Content service protocols give access to content services, such as content adaptation and dynamic page assembly, distributed through a content network.

end-user mapping with edns client subnet.term: End-user mapping with EDNS client subnet
end-user mapping with edns client subnet.text: End-user mapping lets a CDN use the client's subnet, passed in the edns-client-subnet DNS option, to pick a nearby edge server.

multi-cdn.text: Multi-CDN means a content provider combines several CDN services instead of relying on a single one.

edge computing.text: Edge computing is a distributed computing model that brings computation and data storage closer to the sources of data, and so to users.

subresource integrity.text: Subresource Integrity (SRI) is a W3C recommendation that protects website delivery by validating assets served by a third party, such as a CDN, so they have not been compromised.

cdn security and privacy.text: A CDN can add protection against attacks such as DDoS, but it also brings script-injection and privacy risks.

database.text: An organized collection of data, usually managed by database management software that lets users and applications capture and analyze it.

relational database.text: A database based on the relational model, which stores data in tables of rows and columns.

nosql.text: A type of database design, named for "not only SQL" or "non-relational", that stores and retrieves data differently from the table-based structure of relational databases.

graph database.text: A database that uses graph structures to represent and store data, with nodes for entities, edges for the relationships between them, and properties.

document database.text: A database designed to store, retrieve and manage documents, or semi-structured information, and one of the main categories of NoSQL databases.

elasticsearch.text: A distributed, open search and analytics engine, built on Apache Lucene, for storing, searching and analyzing large volumes of data quickly.

key-value store.text: A data store for storing, retrieving and managing associative arrays (dictionaries), in which each record is stored and found through a unique key.

database management system.text: Software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to a database.

database transaction.text: A unit of work performed in a database management system that is treated in a coherent and reliable way, independent of other transactions.

acid properties.text: A set of four properties of database transactions, atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, intended to guarantee data validity despite errors, power failures and other mishaps.

database models.text: A database model is a type of data model that determines the logical structure of a database and how its data can be stored, organized and manipulated.

isolation.text: The ACID property that determines how a transaction's changes are visible to other users and systems.

primary and foreign keys.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table, and a foreign key is a column that holds the key of a row in another table to link them.

wide-column store.text: A type of NoSQL database that uses tables, rows and columns but lets column names and formats vary from row to row, storing columns in column families.

oltp and olap.text: OLTP systems serve transaction-oriented applications and respond to users in real time, while OLAP systems answer complex analytical queries for reporting and decision support.

data warehouse.text: A central repository of data integrated from disparate sources and organized for reporting and analysis, used by analysts and managers to make decisions.

star and snowflake schemas.text: A star schema is the simplest data warehouse schema: a central fact table of measurements surrounded by dimension tables of descriptive attributes; a snowflake schema normalizes those dimension tables.

online analytical processing.text: An approach to quickly answering multi-dimensional analytical queries, part of business intelligence, in which users analyze data organized in cubes interactively.

connection pooling.text: A connection pool is a cache of reusable database connections managed by the client or middleware.

database languages.text: Special-purpose languages for working with a database, each specific to a particular data model.

sql vs nosql databases.text: The two main kinds of database, SQL (relational) and NoSQL (non-relational), differ in how they are built, what they store and how they store it.

sql.text: A domain-specific language used to manage data, especially in a relational database management system.

spatial database.text: A spatial database is a general-purpose database, usually relational, enhanced with spatial data that represents objects in a geometric space, along with tools for querying and analyzing it.

molap, rolap and holap.text: OLAP systems are traditionally grouped by storage into multidimensional (MOLAP), relational (ROLAP) and hybrid (HOLAP) types.

querying and indexing in nosql.text: How NoSQL databases handle queries on fields that are not indexed, and what indexing features they offer to speed them up.

database constraints.text: Rules that restrict the data that can be stored in the relations of a database.

relational operations.text: The operations of relational algebra, such as selection, projection and join, that express queries against a relational database.

handling relational data in nosql.text: Because most NoSQL databases cannot join in queries, related data is handled by multiple queries, by storing copies of values, or by nesting data.

stored procedure.text: Executable code that is associated with, and generally stored in, the database.

views and materialized views.text: A view is a relation computed from other relations by relational operations rather than one that stores data.

vector database.text: A vector database stores and retrieves embeddings of data in vector space; it is also called a vector store or vector search engine.

choosing a database by workload.text: Pick the kind of database that matches the workload: transactional, analytical, text search, document, key-value, graph, vector or geospatial.

polyglot persistence.text: Using multiple data storage technologies within a single system to meet varying data storage needs.

base consistency model.text: A looser alternative to ACID, built on basic availability, soft state and eventual consistency, that NoSQL databases often adopt to gain scale and resilience.

acid vs base.text: The choice between strict ACID transactions and looser BASE guarantees depends on the application's requirements.

time series database.text: A database optimized for time series data, a sequence of data points indexed in chronological order.

concurrency control.text: The mechanisms in a DBMS that handle isolation and guarantee the correctness of concurrent transactions.

etl and elt.text: Two workflows for loading a data warehouse: ETL transforms data before loading it, while ELT loads raw data into the warehouse and transforms it there.

multi-model database.text: A database management system designed to support multiple data models against a single, integrated backend.

newsql.text: A class of relational database systems that seek the scalability of NoSQL systems for online transaction processing while keeping the ACID guarantees of a traditional database.

multiversion concurrency control.text: A non-locking concurrency control method that keeps multiple versions of each data item so readers see a consistent snapshot while writers write.

n+1 query problem.text: A performance problem where code runs one query plus N additional queries to fetch data that a single query could have returned.

transaction states.text: The states a transaction passes through, from active to committed, or failed and aborted, until it is terminated.

database schema.text: A definition of the shape of a data structure that specifies what kinds of data can go where.

two-phase locking.text: A pessimistic concurrency control method that guarantees conflict-serializability by making each transaction acquire all its locks before releasing any.

postgresql isolation levels.text: PostgreSQL accepts the four standard transaction isolation levels but implements three distinct ones, built on its multiversion concurrency control.

snapshot isolation.text: A guarantee that all reads in a transaction see a consistent snapshot of the database and that the transaction commits only if its updates do not conflict with concurrent updates made since that snapshot.

isolation levels.text: Settings that control how much locking a transaction does when selecting data, trading protection from concurrency effects against concurrency.

database normalization.text: Database normalization is the process of structuring a relational database according to normal forms to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity.

database index.text: A database index is a data structure that speeds up finding rows in a table, at the cost of extra writes and storage to maintain it.

read phenomena in transactions.text: The SQL-92 standard names three read phenomena that can occur when a transaction retrieves data another transaction might have updated.

write skew.text: An anomaly in which two concurrent transactions read an overlapping data set, make disjoint updates and both commit, neither having seen the other's update.

hash table.text: A hash table is a data structure that implements an associative array, mapping keys to values by using a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets.

b-tree.text: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree that keeps data sorted and allows searches, sequential access, insertions and deletions in logarithmic time.

write-ahead log.text: Write-ahead logging is a family of techniques that give a database atomicity and durability: changes are first recorded in an append-only log on stable storage before they are written to the database.

storage engine.text: The storage engine is the part of the database engine responsible for putting data into permanent storage.

inverted index.text: An inverted index is a database index that maps content, such as words, to its locations in a table or in a document or set of documents.

r-tree.text: R-trees are tree data structures for spatial access methods, indexing multi-dimensional information such as geographical coordinates, rectangles or polygons.

insertion, update and deletion anomalies.text: Anomalies are the undesirable side effects that can arise when modifying a relation that has not been sufficiently normalized.

b-trees and disk reads.text: A B-tree index breaks a database into fixed-size pages arranged in levels from a root page down to leaf pages, so a lookup needs only a few disk reads.

b+ tree and b* tree.text: The B+ tree and B* tree are variants of the B-tree that keep all record pointers in the leaves or keep nodes more densely packed.

clustered and non-clustered indexes.text: A clustered index stores a table's rows in the order of the index key, while a non-clustered index is a separate sorted structure that points to rows stored elsewhere.

log-structured merge-tree.text: A log-structured merge-tree (LSM tree) is a data structure that suits indexed access to files with a high insert volume, such as transactional log data.

denormalization.text: Denormalization is a strategy applied to a previously normalized database to increase performance, by adding redundant copies of data or grouping data.

b-tree versus lsm-tree.text: The biggest difference between the two index structures is that a B-tree enables faster reads while an LSM-tree enables fast writes.

index data structures.text: A database index can be built on several data structures, and the best choice depends on the workload.

hash collision resolution.text: Collision resolution is how a hash table copes with keys that hash to the same index; the two common methods are separate chaining and open addressing.

lsm-tree writes and compaction.text: An LSM tree absorbs writes in memory, flushes them to disk as immutable sorted components and later merges those components.

postgresql index types.text: PostgreSQL provides several index types, B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN plus the bloom extension, each using an algorithm suited to different indexable clauses.

skip list.text: A skip list is a probabilistic data structure that gives O(log n) average search and insertion in an ordered sequence of n elements.

b-tree insertion and deletion.text: Insertion into a B-tree starts at a leaf and splits full nodes, while deletion removes a key and then rebalances nodes that fall below the minimum size.

bitmap index.text: A bitmap index stores most of its data as bit arrays and answers queries by performing bitwise logical operations on them.

covering index.text: A covering index is an index that itself contains all the fields a query needs, so the query is answered without reading the table record.

dense and sparse indexes.text: A dense index has an entry for every record of the table, while a sparse index has entries for only some of the records.

indexes and database constraints.text: Databases use indexes to enforce constraints such as UNIQUE, EXCLUSION, PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY.

types of database indexes.text: Beyond the main tree and hash designs, databases use dense, sparse, reverse-key, inverted, primary and secondary indexes, among others.

pessimistic and optimistic locking.text: Locks maintain data consistency and integrity in multi-user environments by preventing simultaneous modifications that could leave data inconsistent.

lsm-tree lookups and range queries.text: A read in an LSM tree checks the in-memory component first and then the disk components from newest to oldest, using Bloom filters to skip components.

database keys.text: A key is a column or group of columns that identifies rows of a table; the main kinds are primary, composite, candidate, foreign, alternate and surrogate keys.

normal forms.text: Normal forms are a ladder of increasingly strict rules for relations, from first normal form to sixth normal form.

composite index column order.text: In an index on several columns, the order of the columns decides which searches the index can serve.

full table scans and index limits.term: Full table scans and index limits
full table scans and index limits.text: A full table scan is a query plan in which the database reads the searched column of every row because no index can be used.

functional dependencies.text: A functional dependency is a relationship between two attributes, typically between the primary key and a non-key attribute of a table.

normalizing a table to 3nf.text: Normalization is a design technique that takes a relational table up through successive normal forms by splitting out data that violates each one.

computer data storage.text: Computer data storage is the retention of digital data using computer components and recording media.

sixth normal form and columnar stores.term: Sixth normal form and columnar stores
sixth normal form and columnar stores.text: A table is in sixth normal form when each row holds the primary key and at most one other attribute.

hard disk drive.text: A hard disk drive (HDD) is an electro-mechanical storage device that stores digital data magnetically on rapidly rotating platters.

volatile memory.text: Volatile memory is computer memory that needs power to keep its contents and quickly loses the stored data when power is interrupted.

non-volatile memory.text: Non-volatile memory is computer memory that retains stored information even after power is removed.

durability.text: In database systems, durability is the ACID guarantee that the effects of committed transactions survive permanently, even through failures and catastrophic events.

storage hierarchy.text: The storage hierarchy ranks storage from primary memory, which the CPU reads directly, down through slower and cheaper secondary, tertiary and offline storage.

flash memory.text: Flash memory is a solid-state chip that maintains stored data without any external power source.

solid-state drive.text: A solid-state drive (SSD) is a storage device that uses integrated circuits, typically NAND flash, to store data persistently.

block storage.text: Block storage divides data into blocks and stores them as separate pieces, each with a unique identifier.

disk failure and error handling.text: Hard disks fail through mechanical damage and media errors, and drives combine error correction and sector remapping to hide most of them.

drive interfaces.text: Storage drives connect to a computer over bus interfaces such as ATA, SATA, SCSI, SAS and Fibre Channel.

storage device characteristics.text: Storage technologies are told apart by core characteristics such as volatility, mutability, accessibility, addressability, capacity and performance.

raid.text: RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) stores the same data on multiple hard disks or SSDs to protect against a drive failure.

iscsi.text: iSCSI is an IP-based storage networking standard that provides block-level access to storage devices by carrying SCSI commands over a TCP/IP network.

data scrubbing.text: Data scrubbing is the periodic reading and checking of every block in a disk array, including blocks not otherwise accessed, to find bad blocks before they are used.

object storage.text: Object storage breaks data files into pieces called objects and stores them in a single repository that can be spread across multiple networked systems.

file storage.text: File storage stores data as files and presents them to users as a hierarchical directory structure.

raid implementations.text: RAID can be implemented by dedicated hardware controllers, by operating system software, or by firmware and drivers on a standard drive controller.

amazon s3.text: Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) is an AWS service that provides object storage through a web service interface.

cloud storage.text: Cloud storage is storage built on highly virtualized infrastructure, offered with cloud-native interfaces and elastic scaling.

das, nas and san.text: Direct-attached storage uses no network, while network-attached storage and storage area networks give a computer access to mass storage over a network.

fibre channel.text: Fibre Channel is a high-speed protocol providing in-order, lossless delivery of raw block data, used mainly to connect servers to storage in storage area networks.

network file system.text: Network File System (NFS) is a distributed file system protocol that lets a client computer access files over a network much like local storage.

server message block.text: Server Message Block (SMB) is a communication protocol used to share files, printers, serial ports and other communications between nodes on a network.

ssd as a cache layer.text: SSDs can serve as a fast cache layer in front of slower hard-disk-based storage.

ssd endurance.text: SSD endurance is how much writing a drive can take, listed on its datasheet as drive writes per day or as terabytes written.

wear leveling and trim.text: Wear leveling is a technique that spreads write and erase operations evenly across all blocks of an SSD's flash memory.

parallel nfs.text: Parallel NFS (pNFS), part of NFSv4.1, separates file metadata from file data so a client can move data directly to and from a set of data servers.

opportunistic locking.text: An SMB opportunistic lock (OpLock) lets a client cache a network file locally to improve performance; it is not a true lock and gives no mutual exclusion.

object stores versus key-value stores.text: An object store resembles a key-value store but adds attributes to each item and is built for large data, so the two differ in metadata, size and consistency.

object storage use cases.text: Object stores are used for archiving, unstructured data, cloud-native storage, data lakes, IoT data, and backup and recovery.

reed-solomon codes.text: Reed-Solomon codes are error-correcting codes, introduced by Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon in 1960, that treat a block of data as symbols of a finite field and add check symbols.

raid levels.text: RAID levels differ in how they combine striping, mirroring and parity, trading capacity, speed and fault tolerance.

erasure coding.text: Erasure coding protects data by splitting it into chunks spread over different servers and adding parities, so lost chunks can be rebuilt.

hadoop distributed file system.text: The Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) is a distributed file system designed to run on commodity hardware.

scalability.text: Scalability is the property of a system to handle a growing amount of work.

high availability.text: High availability is a characteristic of a system that aims to ensure an agreed level of operational performance, usually uptime, for a higher than normal period.

parity check.text: A parity check appends one checksum value to k values, so any single erased value can be recovered.

weaknesses of raid.text: RAID arrays can still be lost when a second drive fails during a long rebuild, when read errors surface, or when a crash leaves parity inconsistent.

redundancy.text: Redundancy is the intentional duplication of critical components or functions of a system to raise its reliability, usually as a backup or fail-safe.

mean time between failures.text: Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the predicted average time between inherent failures of a repairable system during normal operation.

horizontal and vertical scaling.text: Scaling horizontally (out) means adding nodes, while scaling vertically (up) means adding resources such as CPUs, memory or storage to a single node.

stateless and stateful services.text: A stateless protocol is one where the receiver keeps no session state from previous requests, while a stateful protocol may retain it.

amdahl's law.text: Amdahl's law is a formula that limits the speedup of a task as resources are added to the system executing it.

autoscaling.text: Autoscaling is a cloud computing method that automatically adjusts the number of active servers in a server farm to match the load on the farm.

dimensions of scalability.text: Scalability can be measured along several dimensions, such as administrative, functional, geographic, load, generation and heterogeneous scalability.
