diminishing returns of adding hardware.text: Adding processors speeds up a task less and less when part of the work is sequential, as Amdahl's law shows.

scalability strategies.text: Eight common strategies for scaling a system are stateless services, horizontal scaling, load balancing, auto scaling, caching, database replication, database sharding and async processing.

database scaling strategies.text: Database scalability is the ability of a database system to perform additional work when given greater hardware resources, such as more servers, processors, memory and storage.

computer cluster.text: A computer cluster is a group of two or more computers, or nodes, that run in parallel to achieve a common goal.

universal scalability law.text: The Universal Scalability Law models and optimizes the scalability of a distributed system using parameters such as contention and coherency.

availability and the nines.text: Availability is the percentage of time a system is up, usually measured over a year and often quoted in nines.

scale-out storage consistency.text: In scale-out data storage, scalability is the largest cluster size that still guarantees full consistency, meaning only one valid version of the stored data in the whole cluster.

scheduled and unscheduled downtime.text: Downtime is a period when a system is unavailable, and it is either scheduled, usually for maintenance, or unscheduled, usually from a failure.

mean time to repair.text: Mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average time needed to repair a failed component or device, a basic measure of how maintainable a repairable item is.

measuring availability.text: Measured availability depends on interpretation, because what users experience can differ from the uptime an administrator reports.

recovery time and recovery point objecti.term: Recovery time and recovery point objectives
recovery time and recovery point objecti.text: Recovery time, or recovery time objective, is the total time needed to recover fully from an outage and is closely related to availability.

active-active and active-passive cluster.text: The two most common high availability clustering configurations are active-active and active-passive.

availability in sequence and in parallel.term: Availability in sequence and in parallel
availability in sequence and in parallel.text: Components in sequence multiply their availabilities and so lower the total, while components in parallel raise the total.

forms of redundancy.text: Computing uses hardware, information, time and software redundancy, plus dissimilar and geographic variants, to keep a system running when parts fail.

capacity planning.text: Capacity planning is the process of determining the capacity needed to meet changing demand; in IT it estimates the storage, hardware, software and connection resources required over a future period.

replication.text: Replication in computing means maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent.

single point of failure.text: A single point of failure is a part of a system that would stop the entire system from working if it failed.

scalability bottlenecks.text: A scalability bottleneck is a part of the design, such as a centralized, slow or tightly coupled component, that stops a system from growing.

clustering versus load balancing.text: Clustering links servers that work together toward a common purpose, while load balancing spreads requests across servers that are unaware of each other.

failover.text: Failover is when a standby or replica takes over the work of a failed component so that the system keeps operating.

gossip protocol.text: A gossip or epidemic protocol is a procedure of peer-to-peer communication based on the way epidemics spread.

single-leader replication.text: In single-leader (primary/replica) replication, one database instance is the leader that handles all writes and propagates them to replica nodes.

log-shipping standby servers.text: Log shipping builds a high-availability setup in which a standby server continuously replays the primary's write-ahead log and is ready to take over if the primary fails.

leader election.text: Leader election is the process of designating a single process as the organizer of a task distributed among several nodes.

multi-master replication.text: Multi-master replication is a method of database replication in which a group of computers stores the data and any member can update it.

replication conflict resolution.text: When concurrent modifications land on different leader nodes, a replicated database must either prevent the transactional conflict or resolve it afterwards.

conflict-free replicated data type.text: A conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) is a data structure replicated across computers that any replica can update independently and concurrently, with a built-in algorithm that resolves inconsistencies so replicas converge.

synchronous and asynchronous replication.text: Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy to acknowledge a write, while asynchronous replication completes the write once local storage acknowledges it.

quorum.text: A quorum is the minimum number of votes a distributed transaction must obtain before it may perform an operation in a distributed system.

leaderless replication.text: In leaderless replication any replica accepts writes, as in Dynamo, a set of techniques for a highly available key-value store with no distinguished node.

read replica pattern.text: In the read replica pattern, all data-modifying commands go to the primary database and reads go to read replicas.

performance bottleneck.text: A bottleneck occurs when the capacity of an application or computer system is limited by a single component.

replication lag and read-after-write con.text: Replication lag is the delay in propagating changes from the leader to its replicas, which can leave replicas serving stale data.

active and passive replication.text: Active replication processes the same request at every replica, while passive replication processes each request on one replica and transfers the result to the others.

chain replication.text: Chain replication is a family of multi-primary protocols that arrange replicas in a chain for writes to get high throughput and strong consistency.

replication change propagation methods.text: Databases replicate data changes between nodes by shipping SQL statements, the storage engine's write-ahead log, or row-level changes.

logical replication.text: Logical replication replicates data objects and their changes based on their replication identity, usually a primary key, rather than copying physical blocks.

replication models.text: Three widely cited models for data replication are transactional replication, state machine replication and virtual synchrony.

storage replication.text: Storage replication copies block-device updates to several physical disks, so any file system on top is replicated without modification.

split-brain.text: Split-brain is a state of data or availability inconsistency caused by two separate data sets with overlapping scope, typically when servers stop communicating and synchronizing, as in a network partition.

choosing a replication solution.text: Database servers can work together for high availability, by letting a second server take over if the primary fails, or for load balancing, by letting several computers serve the same data.

file-based replication.text: File-based replication copies data at the logical level of individual files rather than at the storage block level.

database partitioning.text: A partition is a division of a logical database or its constituent elements into distinct, independent parts.

state-based and operation-based crdts.text: State-based CRDTs replicate by sending full state to be merged, while operation-based CRDTs replicate by sending the update operations.

common crdt data types.text: Counters and sets are built as CRDTs by giving each replica its own slot or tag and merging with maximum or union operations.

partitioning criteria.text: The rules a database uses to assign each row to a partition from its partitioning key: range, list, composite, round-robin or hash.

range partitioning.text: Range partitioning assigns continuous ranges of the partitioning key to partitions, like the volumes of an encyclopedia.

horizontal partitioning.text: Horizontal partitioning puts different rows of a table into different tables.

database sharding.text: A database shard is a horizontal partition of the data in a database or search engine, and each shard may be held on a separate database server instance.

shared-nothing architecture.text: A shared-nothing architecture is a distributed computing architecture in which each update request is satisfied by a single node (processor, memory and storage unit) in a cluster.

hot spots and data skew.text: Skew is uneven distribution of data or load across partitions, and a partition that receives excessive load is called a hot spot.

consistent hashing.text: A hashing technique that lets a hash table be resized while remapping only about n/m keys on average, where n is the number of keys and m the number of slots.

challenges of sharding.text: Sharding adds complexity to the database infrastructure and application code, which brings several costs: harder queries, more software that can fail, and more demanding failover, backup and schema management.

hash partitioning.text: Hash partitioning applies a hash function to the partitioning key, turning skewed data into a uniform distribution so that load spreads evenly across partitions.

distributed hash table.text: A distributed hash table (DHT) is a distributed system that provides a lookup service similar to a hash table.

rendezvous hashing.text: Rendezvous or highest random weight (HRW) hashing is an algorithm that lets clients reach distributed agreement on a set of k options out of a possible set of n options.

virtual nodes.text: A virtual node (vnode) is an existing physical node mapped multiple times across the hash ring, so that its share of the key space is made of several small ranges.

database federation.text: Federation, also called functional partitioning, splits up databases by function.

chord.text: Chord is a distributed lookup protocol that lets peer-to-peer applications locate the node storing a particular data item.

vertical partitioning.text: Vertical partitioning creates tables with fewer columns and stores the remaining columns in additional tables, so rows are split by their columns.

consistency model.text: A consistency model is a contract between the programmer and a system: if the programmer follows the rules for operations, reads, writes and updates behave predictably.

eventual consistency.text: Eventual consistency is a model used in distributed computing to achieve high availability: if no new updates are made to an item, all reads eventually return its last updated value.

network partition.text: A network partition is a division of a computer network into relatively independent subnets, either by design or because network devices fail.

cap theorem.text: The CAP theorem, also called Brewer's theorem, says a distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees: consistency, availability and partition tolerance.

replica conflict resolution.text: To converge, an eventually consistent system exchanges updates between servers and reconciles concurrent updates by choosing a final state.

pacelc.text: PACELC extends the CAP theorem: during a network partition choose between availability and consistency, and otherwise choose between latency and consistency.

cp, ap and ca systems.text: Because a distributed database must tolerate partitions, it is classed as CP if it keeps consistency, AP if it keeps availability, or CA if it assumes no partitions.

common misreadings of cap.text: The CAP theorem is often misunderstood: the simple '2 of 3' wording can mislead, and the theorem covers only a narrow case.

strong eventual consistency.text: Strong eventual consistency adds a safety guarantee to eventual consistency: any two nodes that have received the same set of updates, in any order, are in the same state.

primary-backup replication.text: In primary-backup replication, each data item has one primary that coordinates its writes, and backups copy the updates.

linearizability.text: In a linearizable system, although operations overlap on a shared object, each operation appears to take place instantaneously; it is also called atomic consistency.

linearization point.text: The point between a call's invocation and its response at which the call appears to occur instantly.

active replication.text: In active replication, every replica has a process that applies each update as an operation, and all replicas must apply updates in the same order.

sequencer.text: A central coordinator that assigns a sequence number to each operation and forwards it to all replicas.

quorum-based replication.text: In quorum-based replication a client must get permission from several servers before it reads or writes replicated data.

sequential consistency.text: Sequential consistency requires that the result of any execution is as if all operations ran in one sequential order, with each process's operations in its program order.

causal consistency.text: Causal consistency weakens sequential consistency by splitting events into causally related ones and unrelated ones, and only the related writes must be seen in the same order.

session guarantees.text: Session guarantees are four consistency models proposed in a 1994 paper for the case where a single user or application makes the data modifications.

pacelc database classifications.text: PACELC rates databases by whether they favour availability or consistency during a partition and latency or consistency otherwise.

eventual consistency patterns.text: Eventual consistency ensures that updates to a distributed database are eventually reflected across all nodes, and four patterns help applications achieve it.

distributed transaction.text: A distributed transaction is a transaction that runs across multiple nodes in a network, depending on where the data lives.

two-phase commit.text: Two-phase commit is a distributed algorithm that makes all participants in a distributed transaction agree on whether to commit or abort it.

lamport timestamp.text: The Lamport timestamp is a simple logical clock algorithm for ordering events in a distributed system.

heartbeat failure detection.text: Heartbeats are periodic signals that let a distributed system monitor the health and status of its components.

consensus.text: Consensus is the problem of getting a number of processes, some of which may fail, to agree on a single data value.

vector clock.text: A vector clock is a data structure that determines the partial ordering of events in a distributed system and detects causality violations.

happened-before relation.text: The happened-before relation orders events by their potential causal relationship in a concurrent system, especially an asynchronous distributed system.

two-phase commit variants.text: Two-phase commit variants keep its guarantees while cutting its messages, log writes or completion time.

distributed lock.text: A distributed lock is a mechanism that ensures mutual exclusion across a distributed system.

state machine replication.text: State machine replication is a technique for converting an algorithm into a fault-tolerant, distributed implementation.

single-value and multi-valued consensus.text: Single-value consensus agrees on one value, while multi-valued consensus agrees on a series of values over time.

synchronous and asynchronous systems.text: In a synchronous system all communication proceeds in rounds, while in an asynchronous system messages have no such round structure.

three-phase commit.text: Three-phase commit is a distributed algorithm that makes all nodes agree to commit or abort a transaction, without the indefinite blocking that two-phase commit can suffer.

two generals' problem.text: The Two Generals' Problem is a thought experiment that illustrates the pitfalls of coordinating an action over an unreliable communication link.

crash and byzantine failures.text: A process can fail by crashing, which means it abruptly stops and never resumes, or by a Byzantine failure, where no conditions are imposed on its behavior.

atomic broadcast.text: Atomic broadcast, or total order broadcast, is a broadcast in which all correct processes receive the same set of messages in the same order.

apache zookeeper.text: Apache ZooKeeper is an open-source server for highly reliable distributed coordination of cloud applications.

flp impossibility result.text: The FLP result proves that in a fully asynchronous system where even one process may crash, no deterministic algorithm can achieve consensus.

paxos.text: Paxos is a family of protocols for solving consensus in a network of unreliable or fallible processors.

byzantine fault tolerance.text: A Byzantine fault is a fault that presents different symptoms to different observers, including imperfect information on whether a component has failed; Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is resilience to such conditions.

raft.text: Raft is a consensus algorithm designed as an alternative to the Paxos family.

consensus-based system patterns.text: Distributed consensus algorithms only let nodes agree on a value once, so they are used inside higher-level components such as datastores, configuration stores, queues, locks and leader election services.

sizing a consensus group.text: Consensus systems use majority quorums, so a group of 2f + 1 replicas tolerates f failures, and the number of replicas is one of the most critical deployment decisions.

placing consensus replicas.text: Where to put the processes of a consensus cluster trades off the failure domains the system should survive against its latency requirements.

basic paxos.text: Basic Paxos is the simplest Paxos protocol: each instance decides a single output value over one or more rounds of two phases.

multi-paxos.text: Multi-Paxos runs a continuous series of Basic Paxos instances, with a stable leader, to agree on a stream of commands for a distributed state machine.

permissioned and permissionless consensu.text: Permissioned consensus runs among a fixed, known group of authenticated participants, while permissionless consensus lets anyone join dynamically.

consensus performance.text: Consensus is often thought too slow for high throughput and low latency, but the SRE book says this is untrue: implementations can be slow, yet a number of techniques improve performance.

monitoring consensus systems.text: Consensus systems are monitored for the number and health of group members, whether a leader exists, how often leadership changes and whether the system makes progress.

cheap paxos.text: Cheap Paxos extends Basic Paxos to tolerate F failures with F + 1 main processors and F auxiliary processors, by dynamically reconfiguring after each failure.

fast paxos.text: Fast Paxos generalizes Basic Paxos to reduce end-to-end message delays.

saga pattern.text: A saga is a sequence of local transactions that together do the work of one distributed transaction.

raft leader election.text: A Raft leader election starts a new term when the leader fails or the algorithm initializes, and the candidate that wins a majority of votes becomes leader.

raft log replication.text: In Raft the leader accepts client requests, appends them to its log and replicates them to the followers.

compensating transaction.text: A compensating transaction is a transaction that reverses the effects of a previously committed transaction.

spanner.text: Google's scalable, multiversion, globally distributed and synchronously replicated SQL database.

amazon dynamo.text: Amazon's highly available key-value store, built for internal use to keep persistent state reliable while components fail all the time.

amazon dynamodb.text: A managed NoSQL database service from AWS that supports key-value and document data and is built for scalability and performance.

bigtable.text: A distributed storage system for structured data designed to scale to petabytes of data across thousands of commodity servers.

dynamodb partition and sort keys.text: The primary key of a DynamoDB table is one or two attributes that uniquely identify each item and decide where it is stored.

dynamodb data modeling patterns.text: A set of ways to lay out data in DynamoDB, chosen to match a workload's access patterns.

apache cassandra.text: An open-source distributed database that handles very large amounts of data across many commodity servers with no single point of failure.

mapreduce.text: A programming model and implementation for processing large data sets on a cluster: the user writes a map function and a reduce function, and the runtime parallelizes the work.

apache hadoop.text: A collection of open-source software utilities for reliable, scalable, distributed computing, built around HDFS storage and MapReduce processing.

hdfs architecture.text: HDFS is Hadoop's distributed, scalable file system that stores large files across many machines, with one NameNode tracking metadata and many DataNodes storing blocks.

apache hbase.text: HBase is an open-source non-relational distributed database modeled after Google's Bigtable and written in Java.

cassandra data model.text: Cassandra stores data in keyspaces of tables whose rows are found by a partition key and may each have different columns.

cassandra gossip and failure handling.text: Cassandra nodes spread cluster state by peer-to-peer gossip and each node detects failed peers on its own.

cassandra write and read path.text: Cassandra writes append to a commit log and an in-memory Memtable, which later flushes to immutable SSTables.

scylladb.text: ScyllaDB is a source-available distributed NoSQL wide-column data store designed to be compatible with Apache Cassandra while reaching significantly higher throughput and lower latency.

bigtable data model.text: Bigtable is a sparse, distributed, multi-dimensional sorted map that maps a row key, a column key and a timestamp to a byte array.

hadoop job scheduling and yarn.text: In first-generation Hadoop a JobTracker hands MapReduce work to TaskTrackers close to the data, and YARN later replaced this engine.

synchronous and asynchronous communicati.text: In synchronous communication the sender waits for a reply, as with an HTTP request; in asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting.

mapreduce dataflow and shuffle.text: A MapReduce job flows through an input reader, map, partition, shuffle, sort, reduce and output writer.

message queue.text: A message queue is a software component, typically used for communication between processes or threads, that holds messages in a queue until the receiver takes them.

message-oriented middleware.text: Message-oriented middleware is software or hardware infrastructure that supports sending and receiving messages between distributed systems.

types of queues.text: A queue is a widely used data structure that takes new elements at one end and gives them back from the other; common variants are FIFO, circular, priority and double-ended queues.

message delivery semantics.text: Delivery semantics describe how many times a message reaches its consumer: at most once, at least once, or exactly once.

benefits of message queues.text: Message queues let a system scale, decouple its components, respond faster and survive failures by putting a buffer between producers and consumers.

message broker.text: A message broker is an intermediary program that translates messages between the messaging protocols of sender and receiver and validates, stores, routes and delivers them.

message queue protocols.text: Message queuing historically used closed proprietary protocols; open standards such as AMQP, STOMP and MQTT now exist for open source implementations.

advanced message queuing protocol.text: AMQP is an open standard application layer protocol for message-oriented middleware.

rabbitmq.text: RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker, written in Erlang, that originally implemented AMQP and supports other protocols through plug-ins.

apache activemq.text: Apache ActiveMQ is an open source message broker written in Java together with a full Java Message Service client.

message queue semantics options.text: Queueing systems let you choose between several semantics, such as durability, time to live, filtering and delivery guarantees, that affect reliability and efficiency.

dead letter queue.text: A dead letter queue is a place where a messaging system stores messages that it cannot or should not deliver.

message queue features.text: Message queues commonly offer delayed delivery, delivery guarantees, dead-letter queues, ordering, poison pills, authentication and task queues.

operating-system message queues.text: Operating systems and applications provide message queues that exist only for that system, such as the UNIX SYS V and POSIX queues and the event queues of graphical interfaces.

amazon simple queue service.text: Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) is a distributed message queuing service from Amazon.

choosing a message queue.text: Choose a message queue by comparing speed, scalability, reliability, durability, ease of use, ecosystem, integration and protocol support.

enterprise service bus.text: An enterprise service bus is an architectural pattern in which a centralized software component performs integrations between applications.

blocking and non-blocking queues.text: A blocking queue algorithm uses locks so a waiting thread is suspended, while a non-blocking algorithm rejects access immediately instead of making the thread wait.

backpressure.text: Backpressure limits the size of a queue so that a growing backlog does not slow down the jobs already in it.

push and pull delivery.text: Consumers either pull messages by repeatedly asking the queue for new ones, or have the queue push each message to them when it arrives.

competing consumers.text: The competing consumers pattern lets several consumers process messages from the same queue at the same time.

publish–subscribe pattern.text: Publish–subscribe is a messaging pattern in which publishers send messages to topics without knowing the receivers, and subscribers receive only the topics they asked for.

cloud messaging patterns.text: Cloud messaging patterns are named designs for how services exchange messages, such as asynchronous request-reply, claim check, saga and competing consumers.

mqtt.text: MQTT is a lightweight publish-subscribe network protocol for machine-to-machine messaging.

advantages of publish–subscribe.text: Publish–subscribe lets publishers and subscribers work independently, avoids polling, and makes it easy to add or remove subscribers.

observer pattern.text: In the observer pattern a subject keeps a list of observers and automatically notifies them of state changes, typically by calling one of their methods.

nats.text: NATS is an open-source messaging system under the stewardship of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

drawbacks of publish–subscribe.text: The main drawbacks of publish–subscribe come from decoupling: delivery is hard to guarantee, and large systems can become unstable.

publish–subscribe message filtering.text: Filtering is how a pub/sub system selects the messages a subscriber receives, by topic, by content, or by both.

publish–subscribe topologies.text: Pub/sub systems connect publishers and subscribers either through a central broker or event bus, or directly in a brokerless arrangement.

message broker versus event streaming pl.term: Message broker versus event streaming platform
message broker versus event streaming pl.text: Message brokers support several messaging patterns with delivery tracking, while event streaming platforms offer pub/sub distribution of stored topic streams at higher scale.

apache kafka.text: Apache Kafka is a distributed event store and stream-processing platform that keeps messages in a durable log so many consumers can read them.

batch processing.text: Batch processing is the running of a software job in an automated and unattended way.

publish–subscribe features.text: Pub/sub services typically add fanout to many kinds of endpoints, durable storage of messages, and authentication of publishers.

message queue versus publish–subscribe.text: A message queue gives each message to one consumer, while publish–subscribe delivers each message to every subscriber of a topic.

stream processing.text: Stream processing is a programming paradigm that treats streams, or sequences of events in time, as the central input and output objects of computation.

apache spark.text: Apache Spark is an open-source unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing.

kafka architecture.text: Kafka organizes messages into topics split into partitions, written by producers, read by consumer groups and stored on a cluster of brokers.

preventing message loss in kafka.text: Kafka can lose messages at the producer, the broker or the consumer unless acknowledgments, replicas and offset commits are configured carefully.

change data capture.text: Change data capture identifies and captures the changes made to data in a database so they can be replicated and synced to other systems.

kafka streams.text: Kafka Streams is a Java library for building stateful, scalable and fault-tolerant stream-processing applications on top of Kafka.

complex event processing.text: Complex event processing infers higher-level events from combinations of simpler events in streams as they arrive.

change data capture methods.text: CDC can detect changes with timestamp, version-number or status columns, with triggers that log events to a queue table, or by reading the database transaction log.

apache flink.text: Apache Flink is an open-source, unified stream-processing and batch-processing framework.

stream processing engines.text: Distributed stream processing engines are grouped by execution model into native continuous engines, micro-batch engines and distributed logging fabrics.

event-driven architecture.text: A way of building a system in which parts communicate by producing and reacting to events, usually through a message broker that publishes and delivers them asynchronously.

domain-driven design.text: Domain-driven design is a software design approach that models software to match a domain according to input from the domain's experts.

event store.text: A database optimized for storing events, where an entity's state at any point in its history is rebuilt by replaying its events in order.

event sourcing.text: Storing the full series of actions taken on data in an append-only event store, instead of just the current state, and treating that store as the source of truth.

fallacies of distributed computing.text: The fallacies of distributed computing are false assumptions that programmers new to distributed applications invariably make, listed by L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems.

broker and mediator topologies.text: The two main ways to wire an event-driven system: a broker topology with no central coordinator, or a mediator topology with one orchestrator that controls the workflow.

error handling and data loss in event-dr.term: Error handling and data loss in event-driven systems
error handling and data loss in event-dr.text: Ways to cope with consumers that fail on an event and with events that get lost in transit between components.

event processing styles.text: Three general ways of processing events, simple, stream and complex, plus online event processing that works over distributed event logs.

event structure and payload design.text: An event has a header describing it and a payload carrying the details of the state change, and the payload can hold either all needed data or only keys.

command–query separation.text: Command–query separation is a principle that every method should be either a command that performs an action or a query that returns data, but not both.

command query responsibility segregation.text: An architectural pattern that divides a system's actions into commands that change state and queries that only read it, with separate interfaces and often separate models for each.

domain events and integration events.text: Two kinds of event: domain events mark occurrences inside one business domain, and integration events carry changes across bounded contexts.

event flow layers.text: The four logical layers an event passes through: producer, channel, processing engine and downstream activity.

event granularity.text: Choosing how many event types to publish and how much each one says, so consumers neither drown in detail nor do needless work.

synchronous request-response over events.text: A way to get a synchronous answer from an event-driven system by pairing each request event with a reply, using queues.

timeout antipattern.text: The difficulty of choosing timeout values in distributed systems, where both short and long timeouts cause trouble.

event correction with a double timeline.term: Event correction with a double timeline
event correction with a double timeline.text: Giving every stored event a valid date and a transaction date so an error is fixed by adding a new event rather than editing the old one.

apache avro.text: Avro is a row-oriented remote procedure call and data serialization framework developed within Apache's Hadoop project.

loose coupling.text: A loosely coupled system is one whose components make little or no use of knowledge of the definitions of other components, so a change in one least affects another.

monolithic application.text: A single, self-contained application designed as one service that performs every step needed for a business function.

event schema evolution.text: Techniques for changing the shape of events over time without breaking the services that produce and consume them.

microservices.text: An architecture that organizes an application into a collection of small, loosely coupled services that communicate through lightweight protocols and can be deployed and scaled independently.

service-oriented architecture.text: An architectural style built from discrete services, each a unit of functionality that can be accessed remotely and updated independently, instead of one monolithic design.

service discovery.text: The process of automatically detecting services on a network, so clients can find service instances whose locations change.

service mesh.text: A dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication using a proxy paired with each service.

distributed tracing.text: A distributed trace is an interrelated series of discrete events, called spans, that track the progression of a single user request through the services that fulfil it.

n-tier architecture.text: An architecture that divides an application into logical layers, each with a specific responsibility, which may run on physically separate tiers.

orchestration versus choreography.text: Two ways microservices collaborate: through shared rules for exchanging messages (choreography) or through a central coordinator that calls and combines the services (orchestration).

service registry and registration.text: A highly available database of the network locations of service instances, kept current by services registering themselves or by a third party doing it for them.

microservices versus soa.text: How microservices relate to service-oriented architecture: sometimes used interchangeably, but differing in scope and aim.

service provider, broker and consumer.text: The three roles in SOA: a provider publishes a service, a broker makes it findable, and a consumer finds and binds to it.

service-oriented design principles.text: A set of published guidelines for designing services that stay loosely coupled, reusable and independent of their consumers.

components of a microservice architectur.text: The usual building blocks around a set of microservices: a load balancer, CDN, API gateway, identity provider, service registry, management component and domain services with their own databases.

client-side and server-side discovery.text: The two main service discovery patterns: the client queries a service registry itself, or it calls a load balancer that finds an instance for it.

microservices best practices.text: A set of working rules for microservices: model them on the business domain, give each its own data, keep couplings loose and plan for failure.

monolith versus microservices.text: The choice between building an application as one deployable unit or as many small independent services, which depends on team, business maturity and latency needs.

bounded context.text: A natural division of business logic with an explicit boundary inside which one domain model is consistent and valid.

cell-based architecture.text: A design that organizes resources into self-contained cells, each running a set of microservices and serving part of the requests, to limit the blast radius of failures.

code sharing between microservices.text: Ways to deal with the need to share code across services in an architecture that ideally shares nothing.

microservice granularity.text: How big or small to make each service, a trade-off between independence and the cost of communication between services.

reach-in reporting antipattern.text: Reporting by pulling data straight out of each microservice's store, which breaks bounded contexts or delivers stale data.

testing and observing microservices.text: Practices that keep many independently deployed services testable and visible: stable interfaces, contract tests and aggregated logs, metrics and traces.

consul.text: Consul is a service networking platform developed by HashiCorp.

distributed monolith.text: A system that looks like microservices but is tightly coupled internally, like a monolithic application.

microservices pitfalls.text: Common mistakes that make a microservices architecture fail to deliver its promised benefits.

modular monolith.text: A single deployed application whose code is split into independent modules, one per feature.

strangler fig pattern.text: The strangler fig pattern wraps old code so that calls are redirected to newer code, or so that uses of the old code are logged.

incremental migration to microservices.text: Replacing parts of a monolith with microservices step by step, moving application code first and decoupling the data later.

rest.text: A software architectural style, created to describe and guide the design of the Web's architecture, that sets constraints for how a distributed, Internet-scale hypermedia system should behave.

api.text: A connection between computers or programs: a software interface through which one piece of software offers a service to other pieces of software.

remote procedure call.text: An action in which a program causes a procedure to run in a different address space, commonly on another computer, written as if it were a normal local call.

graphql.text: A query language and server-side runtime for APIs that gives clients exactly the data they request and no more.

serialization.text: Serialization translates a data structure or object state into a format that can be stored or transmitted and reconstructed later, possibly on another computer.

rest architectural constraints.text: The set of constraints that define the REST architectural style and that a system applies to be considered RESTful.

rest uniform interface.text: The REST constraint, fundamental to any RESTful system, that gives every part of the system one uniform way to interact so that each part can evolve independently.

hateoas.text: Hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS) is a REST constraint under which a client discovers what it can do next from hypermedia links that the server returns.

serialization formats.text: Serialization formats range from compact binary encodings such as XDR to human-readable text encodings such as XML, JSON and YAML.

protocol buffers.text: Protocol Buffers is an open-source, cross-platform data format and interface definition language for serializing structured data in a compact, forward- and backward-compatible way.

grpc.text: A high-performance, open-source Remote Procedure Call framework that can run in any environment.

soap.text: SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol specification for exchanging structured information in web services, usually carried over HTTP.

api documentation.text: A description of what services an API offers and how to use them, aiming to cover everything a client needs to know in practice.

api release policies.text: The ways an API can be released: private, partner or public.

web api.text: An API used in web development, defined as a set of specifications such as HTTP request messages together with the structure of the response messages.

api pagination.text: Returning a large dataset from an API in pieces, which handles large datasets efficiently and improves performance.

api versioning and deprecation.text: Managing changes to a public API so that clients that depend on it keep working.

choosing between rest, graphql and grpc.term: Choosing between REST, GraphQL and gRPC
choosing between rest, graphql and grpc.text: A comparison of the three main API technologies on coupling, chattiness, performance, complexity, caching, code generation, discoverability and versioning, which concludes that none is best for every case.

rpc call sequence.text: The steps by which a remote procedure call travels from the calling code through stubs and the network to the server procedure and back.

graphql schema and type system.text: The schema of a GraphQL service: the types and fields that describe what data can be queried from the API.

graphql operations.text: The three kinds of GraphQL operation: queries that read data, mutations that change it, and subscriptions that push live updates.

openapi specification.text: The OpenAPI Specification is a machine-readable interface definition language for describing, producing, consuming and visualizing web services.

push technology.text: Push technology, or server push, is a way of communicating in which the server, rather than the client, starts the exchange.

polling.text: Polling means repeatedly checking an external device or service for its status, as a synchronous activity driven by the client, to retrieve updated information.

long polling.text: In long polling the client sends a request and the server holds it open until new information is available or a timeout is reached, then responds so the client can immediately ask again.

push notification.text: A push notification is a message pushed from a back-end server or application to a user interface such as a mobile or desktop application.

websocket.text: WebSocket is a communications protocol that gives a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection.

web push.text: Web push is the set of web standards that deliver real-time events such as incoming calls or messages to a user, based on a simple protocol over HTTP/2.

techniques for real-time updates.text: To get real-time updates from an HTTP server, either the browser does the work by polling, or the browser and server cooperate over WebSocket or server-sent events.

websocket opening handshake.text: The WebSocket opening handshake is an HTTP Upgrade request from the client and a 101 response from the server, after which the connection switches to the WebSocket protocol.

websocket frames and messages.text: After the opening handshake WebSocket exchanges messages made of one or more frames, which are either data frames (text or binary) or control frames (Close, Ping, Pong).

websocket proxies and load balancers.text: WebSocket is unaware of proxies and firewalls, but its HTTP-compatible handshake lets it pass through HTTP infrastructure, though some proxies break it.

websocket closing handshake.text: The WebSocket closing handshake is an exchange of Close frames in which either peer asks to close and the other answers before the TCP connection is shut.

notification system architecture.text: A notification system takes notifications from business services, validates and schedules them, and delivers them through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes.

webhooks.text: A webhook is an endpoint in your application server that you hand to an external service as a callback, so the service calls it whenever something interesting happens.

websocket api.text: The WebSocket API is the browser interface through which a web application opens a WebSocket, sends messages and reacts to events.

http streaming.text: HTTP server push, also called HTTP streaming, is a way of sending unsolicited asynchronous data from a web server to a web browser.

server-sent events.text: Server-sent events (SSE) is a server push technology in which a client receives automatic updates over an HTTP connection and the server can start sending data once the connection is established.

xmpp.text: XMPP is an open, XML-based communication protocol for instant messaging, presence information and contact list maintenance, enabling near-real-time exchange of structured data between network entities.

presence information.text: Presence information is a status indicator that conveys the ability and willingness of a potential communication partner to communicate.

websocket security.text: WebSocket security rests on the browser's Origin header, TLS (wss) and server-chosen client authentication, because WebSocket requests are not covered by the same-origin policy.

push message delivery controls.text: Web push lets an application server control how long, how urgently and in what form a push message is held and delivered, through the TTL, Urgency and Topic headers.

reconnect with backoff.text: After an abnormal closure a WebSocket client should wait a random, growing delay before reconnecting, so that many clients do not overwhelm the server.

websocket uris.text: WebSocket defines two URI schemes, ws for unencrypted connections and wss for connections protected by TLS.

websocket extensions.text: WebSocket extensions let implementations opt in to additional protocol features, negotiated during the opening handshake.

websocket masking.text: WebSocket masking is the rule that a client XORs every frame it sends to the server with a random 32-bit key, so a script cannot control how its data looks on the wire.

websocket ping and pong.text: Ping and Pong are WebSocket control frames used as keepalive and heartbeat, to check that the other endpoint is still responsive.

websocket subprotocols.text: A WebSocket subprotocol is an application-level protocol layered over WebSocket messages, which the client and server agree on in the opening handshake.

websocket version negotiation.text: WebSocket version negotiation lets a client request a protocol version in the handshake and the server answer with the versions it supports if it cannot accept it.

comet.text: Comet is a web application model in which a long-held HTTPS request lets a web server push data to a browser without the browser explicitly requesting it.

c10k problem.text: The C10k problem was the problem of optimizing networking stacks to handle ten thousand concurrent clients at the same time.

push service operations and security.text: A push service must hold very many open connections and stored messages, deliver reliably, and be secured with TLS, end-to-end encryption and rate limits.

rate limiting.text: Rate limiting prevents the frequency of an operation from exceeding a defined limit.

fault tolerance.text: Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to contain the propagation of faults and keep operating without failure while some components are faulty.

fault tolerance techniques.text: Fault tolerance techniques use spare or independent components, such as replicas, standbys, load balancing and monitoring, so that a failure does not stop the service.

cascading failure.text: A cascading failure is a failure in a system of interconnected parts in which the failure of one or a few parts causes other parts to fail, growing progressively through positive feedback.

deadline propagation.text: An RPC deadline says how long a request may wait before the caller gives up, and deadline propagation passes the remaining time down the whole call tree.

resource exhaustion.text: Resource exhaustion is a server running out of CPU, memory, threads or file descriptors under load, which can start a cascading failure.

load shedding.text: Load shedding drops some proportion of traffic as a server approaches overload, so the server keeps doing useful work instead of failing.

client-side throttling.text: Client-side throttling lets a client that sees many of its recent requests rejected cap its own outgoing traffic, rather than leaving the backend to reject them.

token bucket.text: The token bucket is an algorithm that checks whether traffic conforms to limits on bandwidth and burstiness, using a bucket that fills with tokens at a fixed rate.

bandwidth throttling.text: Bandwidth throttling is the limiting of the rate of data transfer to or from a network node or device such as a computer or mobile phone.

leaky bucket.text: The leaky bucket is an algorithm based on the analogy of a bucket with a constant leak that overflows if water is poured in faster than it leaks or all at once beyond its capacity.

resilience patterns.text: Resilience patterns are design patterns that limit the damage failures do, so a small error does not snowball into an outage.

fail-fast and fail-safe design.text: A fail-fast component reports at the first point of failure, and a fail-safe design fails in a way that protects people, property or data.

graceful degradation.text: A system with graceful degradation keeps running at reduced functionality or performance after a component fails instead of failing completely.

recovering from a cascading failure.text: Recovering from a cascading failure means identifying it, then adding capacity, reducing load, restarting wedged servers or degrading service until the system stabilizes.

rate limiting algorithms.text: The main rate-limiting algorithms are leaky bucket, token bucket, fixed window, sliding log and sliding window, each with its own advantages and disadvantages.

rate limiting in distributed systems.text: Rate limiting across a cluster of nodes is hard because of inconsistent per-node counters and race conditions on shared counters.

measuring capacity beyond qps.text: Queries per second is often a poor measure of capacity because query costs vary, so capacity is better measured directly in resources such as CPU.

per-customer quotas.text: Per-customer quotas cap the resources each customer of a shared backend may use, so under global overload only misbehaving customers get errors.

request criticality.text: Criticality tags each request with how important it is, so an overloaded backend rejects the least critical traffic first.

cascading failure triggers.text: Cascading failure triggers are the disturbances that start the domino effect in a service already susceptible to it, such as process death, updates, rollouts, growth and drains.

cold cache and slow startup.text: A freshly started process or an empty cache serves requests more slowly than in steady state, which can overload a service that is not provisioned for it.

load testing to failure.text: Load testing to failure pushes each component until it breaks, to learn its breaking point and how it behaves beyond it before an overload hits.

queue management for overload.text: A server's request queue in front of its thread pool should be sized so that, when load exceeds capacity, requests are rejected early instead of waiting.

idempotency.text: An operation is idempotent if applying it several times has the same effect as applying it once.

preventing server overload.text: Preventing server overload combines load testing, degraded responses, rejecting excess requests at several layers and capacity planning, in rough priority order.

circuit breaker.text: A design pattern that wraps calls to a remote service, watches for failures and stops making the calls once failures pass a threshold, so failures do not cascade.

retry strategies.text: Retry strategies set how long a client waits between attempts after a transient error, so network instability is handled without overloading the service.

exponential backoff.text: Exponential backoff is an algorithm that uses feedback to multiplicatively decrease the rate of a process, to gradually find an acceptable rate.

retry budgets.text: A retry budget limits retries per request, per client or per server so retries cannot amplify an overload into a cascading failure.

exactly-once execution.text: An operation is executed exactly once when it runs at least once and at most once at the same time.

idempotency keys.text: An idempotency key is a unique value, usually a UUID, that a client sends with a request that is not naturally idempotent so the server can detect duplicates.

circuit breaker states.text: A circuit breaker is in one of three states, closed, open or half-open, which decide whether calls reach the protected service.

backoff jitter.text: Jitter adds randomness to backoff delays so that many senders or clients that fail together do not retry at the same moment.

truncated exponential backoff.text: Truncated exponential backoff caps the number of increases so that the delay stops growing after a limit.

idempotency use cases.text: Idempotency is essential wherever an operation might be retried or executed multiple times.

hierarchical token bucket.text: The hierarchical token bucket is an arrangement of token buckets in a hierarchy that limits each client's rate so that no client saturates the total bandwidth.

idempotent consumers.text: An idempotent consumer handles a message that arrives more than once so that the repeat has no extra effect.

traffic shaping and policing.text: Traffic policing drops or downgrades traffic that exceeds a limit, while traffic shaping delays it until it conforms.

token bucket versus leaky bucket.text: The token bucket and the leaky bucket as a meter are mirror images that classify exactly the same traffic as conforming, while the leaky bucket as a queue is a different, shaping-only variant.

disaster recovery.text: Disaster recovery is the process of regaining access to infrastructure and systems after a natural disaster, cyber attack or other business disruption.

backup.text: A backup is a copy of computer data taken and stored elsewhere so it can be used to restore the original after a data loss event.

data integrity.text: Data integrity means that services remain accessible to users with accurate data, because to users data loss, corruption and extended unavailability look the same.

monitoring.text: Monitoring is collecting, processing, aggregating and displaying real-time quantitative data about a system, such as query counts and types, error counts and types, processing times and server lifetimes.

service level objective.text: A service-level objective (SLO) is a target value or range of values for a service level, measured by a service level indicator.

service level indicator.text: A service level indicator (SLI) is a measure of the service level a provider delivers to a customer.

service-level agreement.text: A service-level agreement (SLA) is an agreement, typically a binding contract, between a service provider and a customer that sets the quality, availability and responsibilities of a service as contract terms.

recovery point objective.text: The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last recovery point, that is, the longest interval of data loss tolerated.

backup methods.text: Backup methods differ in what each backup copies: complete data, changes since the last full backup, changes since the last backup of any kind, or every change as it happens.

recovery time objective.text: The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable delay between an interruption of service and its restoration.

hot, warm and cold sites.text: A backup site is hot if it operates before a disaster, warm if it is ready to begin operating, and cold if it needs substantial work to begin operating.

defense in depth for data integrity.term: Defense in depth for data integrity
defense in depth for data integrity.text: Defense in depth protects data with multiple layers, each guarding against progressively less common loss scenarios, because no silver bullet covers the many combinations of failure modes.

replication is not backup.text: Replication is not recoverability: datastores that automatically sync replicas push a corrupt row or errant delete to every copy, likely before the problem can be isolated.

soft deletion.text: Soft deletion marks deleted data immediately, making it unusable except by the application's administrative code paths, and destroys it after a reasonable delay.

backend subsetting.text: Subsetting limits the pool of backend tasks a client connects to, because each connection costs memory and CPU at both ends, and too many connections per client or per backend waste resources for little gain.

lame duck state.text: A backend in lame duck state is listening and able to serve but explicitly asks clients to stop sending requests, and it broadcasts that fact to all its active clients.

limits of simple round robin.text: Simple round robin sends each client's requests in turn to the connectable, non-lame-duck backends in its subset; it beats random selection but can leave up to a 2x spread in CPU between the least and most loaded task.

virtual ip load balancing.text: A virtual IP address is shared across many devices rather than assigned to one network interface, so users see one regular IP address while a network load balancer forwards packets to a machine behind it.

error budget.text: An error budget is the rate at which a service may miss its SLOs, giving an objective measure of how unreliable the service is allowed to be within a period.

reliability versus cost.text: Past a certain point, increasing a service's reliability makes things worse for the service and its users, because extreme reliability limits feature development and delivery and sharply raises cost.

four golden signals.text: The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors and saturation; if you can measure only four metrics of a user-facing system, measure these.

choosing service level indicators.text: Choosing indicators means selecting a handful of metrics that reflect what users want from the system, rather than every metric a monitoring system can track.

choosing slo targets.text: Choosing SLO targets is not a purely technical activity, because product and business implications shape the SLIs and SLOs, and SRE advises on the risks and viability of options.

chaos engineering.text: Chaos engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent conditions in production.

business continuity planning.text: Business continuity planning is the process of creating systems of prevention and recovery to deal with potential threats, so an organization can keep delivering products or services at acceptable levels after a disruptive incident.

high availability architectures.text: High availability architectures pair a node with a standby, secondary or second primary so the service keeps answering when one node fails.

observability.text: Observability is the ability to ask arbitrary questions about a system without knowing ahead of time what to ask; logging, tracing and metrics are its three pillars.

site reliability engineering.text: Site reliability engineering (SRE) is a discipline that applies software engineering to IT infrastructure and operations to monitor and improve the availability and performance of deployed software systems.

3-2-1 backup rule.text: The 3-2-1 rule says to keep at least 3 copies of the data, on 2 different types of storage media, with one copy offsite in a remote location.

tiered backup strategy.text: A tiered backup strategy keeps frequent, quickly restored backups near the live datastores and fewer, longer-retained backups on more remote, more independent storage.

backing up live data.text: Files being actively updated are hard to back up consistently; one way is to quiesce them, take a snapshot, resume live operations and back up the snapshot.

disaster recovery strategies.text: A disaster recovery strategy is the set of measures chosen to restore systems and data after a disaster, derived from the business continuity plan.

testing data recovery.text: Recovery dependencies, mostly backups, can be latently broken without anyone knowing until recovery is attempted, so recovery must be tested continuously.

disaster recovery practices.text: Disaster recovery practices are the controls, tests and procedures that keep a recovery plan working when a disaster happens.

backups versus archives.text: The most important difference between backups and archives is that backups can be loaded back into an application while archives cannot, so a backup effort should focus on data recovery.

data loss failure modes.text: Data loss failures vary in root cause, scope and rate, giving 24 distinct types that a data integrity program should consider and a restore plan must handle in any combination.

out-of-band data validation.text: Out-of-band data validation is a system of checks and balances within and between an application's datastores that detects low-grade corruption or loss before it becomes unrecoverable.

point-in-time recovery.text: Point-in-time recovery restores each affected artifact to its own unique point in time, possibly for millions of users across days, weeks or months; Google calls it time-travel.

least-loaded round robin.text: Least-loaded round robin has each client track its active requests to every backend in its subset and round robin among the backends with the fewest.

weighted round robin with backend feedba.term: Weighted round robin with backend feedback
weighted round robin with backend feedba.text: Weighted round robin uses backend-provided information: each client keeps a capability score per backend and distributes requests round robin in proportion to those scores.

packet forwarding in network load balanc.term: Packet forwarding in network load balancers
packet forwarding in network load balanc.text: A network load balancer can forward a packet to its chosen backend by network address translation, by changing the data link layer destination, or by encapsulating the packet in another IP packet.

managing expectations with slos.text: Publishing SLOs sets expectations for system behavior, so users can tell whether a service fits their use case.

request-based availability.text: Request-based availability defines availability as the proportion of requests that succeed over a rolling window, instead of the proportion of time a system is up.

setting an availability target.text: A service's availability target depends on its function and market position: what users expect, whether it ties to revenue, whether it is paid or free, what competitors offer, and whether it serves consumers or enterprises.

multiple service levels for infrastructu.text: Infrastructure has multiple clients with varying needs, so a cost-effective answer is to partition it and offer it at multiple independent levels of service.

borg.text: Borg is a distributed cluster operating system that runs users' jobs, either long-running servers or batch processes, as sets of identical tasks on a cluster's machines.

life of a request.text: A user request to a large serving stack passes through DNS, a global load balancer, a reverse-proxy frontend, application frontend and backend servers, and a storage layer such as Bigtable before the reply is assembled.

n+2 capacity planning.text: Sizing a service divides expected peak load by what one task can handle, then adds spare tasks so peak load is still served during updates and machine failures (N+2).

sla components.text: A well-defined SLA contains the type of service, the desired performance level, monitoring and reporting, steps for reporting issues, response and resolution time frames, and repercussions for missed commitments.

cloud service level agreements.text: Cloud SLAs are service-based agreements that cover a shared infrastructure rather than agreements with one customer.

black-box and white-box monitoring.text: Black-box monitoring tests externally visible behavior as a user would see it, while white-box monitoring uses metrics exposed by the system's internals, such as logs or an HTTP handler emitting statistics.

alerting and paging practice.text: Good alerting pages a human only for an urgent, actionable condition that is actively or imminently user-visible, giving good signal and very low noise.

incident management.text: Incident management is the process of limiting the disruption an incident could cause to operations, services or functions, followed by a return to business as usual.

sre team models.text: SRE teams are organized in several models: kitchen sink, infrastructure, product or application, embedded and consulting.

business impact analysis.text: A business impact analysis identifies and evaluates the effects of disruptions on operations and determines the recovery priorities and strategies the organization needs.

disaster recovery tiers.text: Disaster recovery tiers grade recovery solutions from no off-site data up to highly automated recovery, from SHARE's seven tiers of 1992 that IBM updated to eight in 2012.

kubernetes.text: Kubernetes, also known as K8s, is an open-source container orchestration system for automating software deployment, scaling and management.

containers.text: A container is an isolated user-space instance that the operating system kernel allows alongside others, packaging an application with its dependencies so it runs the same in any environment.

chroot.text: chroot is a Unix command and system call that changes the apparent root directory for the current process and its children.

cgroups.text: Cgroups, short for control groups, is a Linux kernel feature that limits, accounts for and isolates the resource usage (CPU, memory, disk I/O and so on) of a collection of processes.

linux namespaces and cgroups.text: Namespaces and cgroups are the Linux kernel features that isolate containers: namespaces control what a process can see, cgroups how much of the system's resources it can use.

pod lifecycle.text: A Pod starts in the Pending phase, moves to Running once at least one primary container starts, and ends in Succeeded or Failed depending on whether any container terminated in failure.

container probes.text: A probe is a periodic check the kubelet runs on a container, so Kubernetes can restart the container when it is unhealthy or stop sending it traffic when it is not ready.

docker.text: Docker is a platform that packages software into containers using operating system-level virtualization.

container images and registries.text: A container image is a read-only template used to build containers, and a registry is a repository that stores and serves images.

container orchestration.text: Container orchestration automates deploying, scaling and managing containers so that, for example, a container that goes down is replaced by another without downtime.

kubernetes nodes.text: A Kubernetes node, also called a worker or minion, is a machine where containers are deployed.

kubernetes pods.text: A pod is the basic deployable unit in Kubernetes, made of one or more containers co-located on the same node.

container runtime.text: A container runtime is the software responsible for the lifecycle of containers, including launching, reconciling and killing them.

pod restart policy.text: The restartPolicy in a Pod spec tells Kubernetes whether to restart a container after it exits, and can be Always, OnFailure or Never.

crashloopbackoff.text: CrashLoopBackOff is the condition of a container that fails to start properly and keeps failing and restarting while Kubernetes delays each restart with an exponential backoff.

graceful pod termination.text: When a Pod is deleted, the kubelet first asks its containers to stop with a TERM signal and only sends KILL once a grace period has expired, so processes can clean up.

container persistent storage.text: Container filesystems are ephemeral by default, so data that must outlive a container needs a volume that provides persistent storage.

kubernetes services.text: A Kubernetes service is a set of pods that work together, such as one tier of a multi-tier application, giving them a stable address.

sidecar and init containers.text: A Pod can hold several tightly coupled containers, such as init containers that run first and sidecar containers that support the main application.

labels and selectors.text: Labels are keys that Kubernetes clients attach to any API object, such as pods and nodes, and label selectors are queries that resolve to the matching objects.

kubernetes service types.text: A Kubernetes Service type says how a Service is exposed: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer or ExternalName, with headless Services as a variant.

kubernetes ingress.text: An Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services inside it, using rules defined on the Ingress resource.

ingress path and host matching.text: Ingress rules choose a backend by matching the request's host and URL path, using a path type of Exact, Prefix or ImplementationSpecific.

docker run workflow.text: Running a container with Docker means the client asks the daemon to pull an image from a registry, create a container from it and start it.

virtual machine.text: A virtual machine is the virtualization or emulation of a computer system that provides the functionality of a physical computer.

hypervisor.text: A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, is software, firmware or hardware that creates and runs virtual machines.

docker compose.text: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications.

docker swarm.text: Docker Swarm provides native clustering for Docker containers, turning a group of Docker engines into a single virtual Docker engine.

virtualization versus containerization.text: Virtual machines virtualize hardware and each carry a guest operating system, while containers virtualize the operating system and carry only the application and its dependencies.

continuous delivery.text: Continuous delivery is a software engineering approach in which teams produce software in short cycles, ensuring that it can be reliably released at any time.

virtual machine snapshots and migration.text: A snapshot is the state of a virtual machine, and generally its storage devices, at an exact point in time, which can be restored later.

physical, virtual and container deployme.text: Applications moved from physical servers to virtual machines to containers as each step gave better resource boundaries and utilization.

ci/cd pipeline.text: CI/CD combines the practices of continuous integration and continuous delivery or, less often, continuous deployment.

release engineering.text: Release engineering is the discipline of building and delivering software, defining every step from source storage and build rules to testing, packaging and deployment.

infrastructure as code.text: Infrastructure as code is managing and provisioning data center resources through machine-readable definition files rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools.

twelve-factor app.text: The twelve-factor app is a set of twelve best-practice principles for building modern applications that are reliable, scalable and manageable.

configmaps and secrets.text: ConfigMaps and Secrets are two closely related Kubernetes mechanisms for storing configuration, so that changes can be made without rebuilding the application.

hermetic builds.text: A hermetic build is insensitive to the software installed on the build machine, so the same revision always produces the same result.

release branching and cherry-picking.text: Release branching cuts a branch from the mainline at one revision and fixes it only by cherry-picking bug fixes, so the release contents stay known.

release pipeline.text: A release pipeline turns a tested source revision into a deployable package by branching, building, testing, packaging and canarying, logging each step.

horizontal pod autoscaler.text: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler automatically updates a workload resource such as a Deployment or StatefulSet to scale capacity to match demand.

autoscaler flapping controls.text: Autoscaler flapping controls are settings that keep the replica count from swinging up and down as metrics fluctuate.

pod resource requests and limits.text: A container can declare how much CPU and memory it needs and how much it may use, which drives scheduling and enforcement.

rolling update.text: A rolling update replaces instances of the old version one by one with the new version, keeping the application available throughout.

deployments and replicasets.text: A ReplicaSet keeps a stable set of replica pods running at any given time, and a Deployment is the higher-level mechanism that manages ReplicaSets.

scaling to zero.text: Scaling to zero lets an autoscaler reduce an idle workload to no replicas and bring it back when a metric shows demand.

kubernetes control plane.text: The Kubernetes control plane manages the cluster's workload and its worker nodes and directs communication across the system.

kubernetes controllers.text: A Kubernetes controller is a reconciliation loop that drives the actual cluster state toward the desired state by creating, updating and deleting the resources it manages.

statefulsets.text: A StatefulSet is a Kubernetes controller that enforces uniqueness and ordering among the instances of a pod so that stateful applications can run.

pod templates.text: A pod template is the specification a workload controller uses to create the Pods it manages.

kubernetes operators.text: A Kubernetes Operator is the combination of custom resources and custom controllers that automates how a particular application is run.

etcd.text: etcd is a persistent, lightweight, distributed key-value data store, originally developed as part of CoreOS.

ingress controllers and classes.text: An Ingress controller carries out the Ingress rules, and an IngressClass tells each Ingress which controller should implement it.

feature toggle.text: A feature toggle is a condition in the code that enables or disables a feature at runtime, as an alternative to maintaining multiple feature branches.

configuration distribution models.text: Configuration can reach a running service in several ways, each trading flexibility, simplicity and drift between the stored and running version.

blue-green deployment.text: A way of installing changes by keeping a live production environment and an idle staging copy, then swapping the two so the staged version goes live.

deployment strategies.text: Deployment strategies are different ways of replacing a running application version with a new one, each managing the update differently.

authentication.text: Authentication is the act of proving an assertion, such as the identity of a computer system user.

canary release.text: A canary release exposes a new version or feature to a small set of users first, so it can be tested incrementally before a wider rollout.

cross-site scripting.text: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a web-application vulnerability that lets attackers inject client-side scripts into pages viewed by other users.

risk-based rollouts.text: A risk-based rollout fits how fast and how widely a release is pushed to the risk profile of the service being updated.

oauth 2.0.text: OAuth 2.0 is an open standard for access delegation that lets a user grant an application consented access to resources on another site without sharing credentials.

authentication factors.text: Authentication factors are the three categories of evidence used to verify identity: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is.

cryptographic salt.text: A salt is random data fed as an additional input to a one-way function that hashes a password or passphrase.

authorization.text: Authorization is the function of specifying rights to access resources, usually through an access policy, and then deciding whether a particular subject may access a particular resource.

principle of least privilege.text: The principle of least privilege requires that every module, such as a process, user or program, be able to access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.

multi-factor authentication.text: Multi-factor authentication grants a user access only after they present two or more distinct types of evidence, or factors, to an authentication mechanism.

oauth pseudo-authentication.text: Pseudo-authentication means using OAuth on its own as a login method, even though OAuth is an authorization protocol that says nothing about who the user is.

continuous authentication.text: Continuous authentication keeps monitoring and verifying a user throughout a session, based on biometric traits, instead of only at the initial log-in.

access control models.text: Access control models are the ways an authorization policy is expressed and checked, such as access control lists, roles, attributes and relationships.

secure system design checklist.text: Designing secure systems protects sensitive information and keeps the infrastructure stable and reliable, so developers should apply security guidelines by default.

session and token authentication.text: A website manages a logged-in user's identity with sessions, tokens, JSON Web Tokens, single sign-on, OAuth 2.0 or QR-code login.

digital authentication.text: Digital authentication, also called electronic authentication, is a group of processes that establish and present confidence in user identities to an information system by electronic methods.

cross-site request forgery.text: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is an exploit in which a web application receives unauthorized commands from a user that it trusts.

access token.text: An access token is a credential, usually an opaque string, representing an authorization issued to the client for accessing protected resources.

refresh token.text: A refresh token is a credential the authorization server issues to the client for obtaining new access tokens.

json web token.text: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is an Internet standard for creating data, optionally signed and optionally encrypted, whose JSON payload asserts a number of claims.

openid connect.text: OpenID Connect is a thin authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds login and profile information about the person who is logged in.

jwt claims.text: The claims of a JWT are the name/value members of the JSON object, called the JWT Claims Set, that the token conveys.
