creating and validating a jwt.text: Creating a JWT builds a claims set and then signs or encrypts it, and validating one reverses those steps and rejects the token if any step fails.

salted password hashing.text: A system stores each password as a hash of the password plus a unique random salt, never as plain text or a bare hash.

rainbow table.text: A rainbow table is a precomputed table of cryptographic hash outputs, usually used to recover passwords from stolen hashes.

oauth 2.0 authorization flow.text: In the OAuth 2.0 flow a client obtains an access token from the authorization server, with the resource owner's consent, and uses it to request resources from the resource server.

oauth 2.0 grant types.text: An authorization grant is a credential representing the resource owner's authorization that the client uses to obtain an access token; RFC 6749 defines four grant types and a way to add more.

authorization code grant.text: The authorization code grant is a redirection-based flow that obtains access and refresh tokens via the user-agent and is optimized for confidential clients.

proof key for code exchange.text: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is an OAuth 2.0 extension that stops an attacker who intercepts an authorization code from redeeming it, by binding the code to a one-time secret only the real client holds.

webauthn.text: WebAuthn is a W3C web standard defining an API that websites use to authenticate users with public-key credentials, commonly called passkeys.

zero trust security model.text: Zero trust is a security strategy in which users and devices are not trusted by default, even on a privileged network such as a corporate LAN or if previously verified.

signed, encrypted and nested jwts.text: A JWT is carried either as a signed JWS or an encrypted JWE, may nest one inside the other, and can also be left unsecured.

argon2.text: Argon2 is a key derivation function that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition.

bcrypt.text: bcrypt is a password-hashing function, based on the Blowfish cipher, designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières.

single sign-on.text: Single sign-on is an authentication scheme in which a user logs in once, with a single set of credentials, to reach several related but independent applications.

mfa bypass attacks.text: MFA can still be bypassed through phishing, SIM swapping, fatigue attacks and implementation flaws.

identity provider.text: An identity provider is a centralized trusted system that stores and manages user identities and authenticates users on behalf of other applications.

kerberos.text: Kerberos is a ticket-based network authentication protocol that lets nodes on a non-secure network prove their identity to one another securely.

openid.text: OpenID is an open, decentralized authentication protocol that lets users sign in to many sites through a third-party identity provider.

url shortening.text: URL shortening makes a long URL substantially shorter while it still leads to the same page, by using a redirect that points to the page with the long URL.

saml.text: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an open XML-based standard for sharing identity, authentication and permission information between systems, such as an identity provider and a service provider.

drawbacks of url shortening.text: Short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot and privacy risks.

short link expiration.text: Some providers let a shortened URL expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses.

base62 encoding.text: Base62 writes numbers with 62 symbols: the capital letters A-Z, the lower case letters a-z and the digits 0-9.

short url key generation.text: A shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key, the part after the domain name, that it builds from letters and digits.

pastebin.text: A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link.

instant messaging.text: Instant messaging is synchronous communication that sends messages in real time between two or more parties over the Internet or another computer network.

end-to-end encryption.text: A way of building a secure communication system in which only the sender and the intended recipients can read the messages.

store and forward.text: A technique in which data is sent to an intermediate station that keeps it in storage and sends it on later to its destination or to another intermediate station.

signal protocol.text: A non-federated cryptographic protocol, formerly called the TextSecure Protocol, that provides end-to-end encryption for voice and instant messaging conversations.

end-to-end encryption versus provider ac.text: The disagreement over whether providers, governments and employers should be able to read messages, set against the privacy that end-to-end encryption gives users.

messaging metadata and sealed sender.text: Encrypting message content does not hide who talks to whom and when, and sealed sender is a technique that reduces the metadata a server can see by concealing the sender's identifier.

chat application on redis pub/sub.text: A simple chat application can be built on Redis publish-subscribe, with the server publishing each chat message to a topic that subscribers pick up.

feed fan-out models.text: Ways to build each user's feed: push a tweet into followers' feeds when it is posted, pull it when the feed is read, or combine both.

apache lucene.text: A free and open-source search engine software library, originally written in Java.

fan-out.text: In messaging middleware, a pattern that delivers one message to one or several destinations, possibly in parallel, without waiting for a response.

feed ranking.text: Scoring each item in a feed by how relevant it is to a specific user, so the most relevant appear first.

edgerank.text: The name commonly given to the algorithm Facebook used to decide which posts to show in a user's News Feed.

trending topics.text: Showing the queries, hashtags and topics searched most often in a recent window.

streaming media.text: Delivering multimedia over a network as a stream of packets that is played in real time or near real time, instead of downloading the whole file first.

adaptive bitrate streaming.text: A technique that encodes video at several bit rates and lets the player switch between them as bandwidth, CPU and device conditions change.

recommender system.text: A type of information filtering system that suggests the items most relevant to a particular user, such as what to watch next.

collaborative filtering.text: A recommendation technique that predicts a user's interests from the preferences of many other users, assuming people who agreed before will agree again.

video codec.text: Software or hardware that compresses and decompresses digital video, usually following a standard video coding format.

http live streaming.text: A protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data over HTTP, in which the client downloads a playlist and the media segments it lists, adapting bit rate to network conditions.

mpeg-dash.text: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, an international-standard adaptive bitrate technique that streams media from conventional HTTP web servers.

video transcoding.text: Converting video by decoding it to an intermediate uncompressed format and re-encoding it into a target format and quality for different devices.

video on demand.text: A media distribution system that lets users access television shows, films and videos digitally on request.

live streaming.text: Delivering video over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.

streaming delivery methods.text: The ways a stream reaches many viewers: separate unicast copies, a single multicast stream, peer-to-peer transfer, or CDN servers.

real-time messaging protocol.text: A protocol for streaming audio, video and data over the Internet, originally built by Macromedia for Flash Player and running over TCP.

h.264.text: Advanced Video Coding (AVC, H.264, MPEG-4 Part 10), a block-oriented, motion-compensated video compression standard.

hevc.text: High Efficiency Video Coding (H.265, MPEG-H Part 2), a patent-encumbered video compression standard published in 2013 as the successor to H.264/AVC.

av1.text: AOMedia Video 1, an open, royalty-free video coding format from the Alliance for Open Media, designed for video transmission over the Internet as the successor to VP9.

geo-blocking.text: Technology that restricts access to Internet content based on the user's geographical location.

nearest neighbor search.text: The optimization problem of finding the point in a given set that is closest, or most similar, to a given query point.

proximity service.text: A service that returns the places within a given radius of a location, such as nearby restaurants.

dynamic pricing.text: A pricing strategy, also called surge pricing, in which flexible prices are set from current market demand, rising at peak demand and falling at low demand.

web crawler.text: An Internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web, usually run by search engines to index the pages it downloads.

robots exclusion protocol.text: The standard, usually called robots.txt, by which a website tells visiting web crawlers which portions of the site they may visit.

crawl politeness policy.text: The rules a crawler follows to avoid overloading the websites it visits.

crawl re-visit policy.text: The rule that decides when a crawler checks pages again for changes, to keep its stored copies from going stale.

crawl selection policy.text: The rule that decides which pages a crawler downloads, ranking pages by an importance metric because only a fraction of the web can be fetched.

search engine indexing.text: The collecting, parsing and storing of data so that information can be retrieved quickly and accurately.

pagerank.text: A link analysis algorithm, used by Google Search, that gives each page in a hyperlinked set a numerical weight measuring its relative importance.

cosine similarity.text: A measure of similarity between two non-zero vectors: the cosine of the angle between them, which is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths.

sitemaps.text: An XML protocol that lets a webmaster tell search engines which URLs on a site are available for crawling.

deep web crawling.text: Reaching the large share of web pages that sit behind queries to a database and have no links pointing to them.

focused crawler.text: A crawler that tries to download only pages similar to a given query or topic, also called a topical crawler.

url normalization.text: Modifying and standardizing a URL in a consistent way, also called URL canonicalization, so that one resource has one form.

spider trap.text: A set of web pages that makes a crawler issue an infinite number of requests or crash, whether built on purpose or by accident.

jaccard index.text: A statistic of how similar two sets are: the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union.

w-shingling.text: A set of unique shingles, each a run of w contiguous tokens from a document, used to measure how similar two documents are.

heap.text: A tree-based data structure in which each parent's key is at least (max heap) or at most (min heap) its children's keys, so the highest- or lowest-priority element always sits at the root.

open banking.text: Open banking lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through application programming interfaces (APIs).

doubly linked list.text: A linked data structure of sequentially linked nodes, each holding a data field plus links to the previous and the next node.

social graph.text: A graph that represents social relations between entities; it is a model of a social network.

adjacency matrix.text: A square matrix representing a finite graph, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent.

adjacency list.text: A graph representation that stores, for each vertex, an unordered list of its neighbours.

breadth-first search.text: A graph or tree search that starts at a root and explores all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next depth level.

shortest path problem.text: Finding a path between two vertices of a graph so that the sum of the weights of its edges is as small as possible.

bidirectional search.text: A graph search that finds a shortest path from a start vertex to a goal by running one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal, stopping when the two meet.

six degrees of separation.text: The idea that all people are six or fewer social connections apart, so a chain of friend-of-a-friend links joins any two people.

simple mail transfer protocol.text: SMTP is the Internet standard protocol that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail.

virtual private cloud.text: An on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources inside a public cloud that isolates one organization's resources from the others.

email message format.text: An Internet email message is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, in the syntax RFC 5322 specifies.

mime.text: MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) extends the email format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments.

email spam.text: Email spam is unsolicited messages sent in bulk by email.

smtp mail transaction.text: An SMTP mail transaction hands one message to a server in three steps: MAIL, one or more RCPT, then DATA.

smtp envelope versus message header.text: A mail object has an envelope that SMTP uses for delivery and content made of a header section and a body.

email header fields.text: Email header fields fall into groups: originator, destination, identification, informational, trace and resent fields.

smtp queueing and retries.text: An SMTP sender keeps mail that cannot be sent at once in a queue and retries it periodically until it succeeds or gives up.

bounce messages.text: A bounce message is the notice an SMTP server sends the originator when it accepted a message but cannot deliver it.

mail agents and relays.text: Mail passes through user agents, submission agents, transfer agents and delivery agents, each with its own role.

mx record.text: An MX record is a DNS resource record naming the mail server responsible for accepting email on behalf of a domain.

post office protocol.text: POP is an application-layer Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve email from a mail server.

email delivery.text: Email travels from the sender's mail client through submission and transfer servers, found with DNS MX records, to the recipient's mailbox.

internet message access protocol.text: IMAP is an Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve and manage messages on a mail server over a TCP/IP connection.

pop versus imap.text: POP downloads mail to one device, whereas IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server so many clients can share it.

imap commands and responses.text: An IMAP session is a text dialogue in which the client sends tagged commands and the server returns data and a tagged completion result.

imap unique identifiers.text: An IMAP unique identifier (UID) is a number that identifies a message in a mailbox, stable across sessions when paired with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY.

email spoofing.text: Email spoofing is designing a message's header so it appears to come from a known or trusted source.

smtp security.text: SMTP security covers authenticating clients, encrypting server-to-server connections and declaring a domain's TLS policy.

spam filtering.text: Spam filtering combines techniques that detect and refuse unsolicited bulk mail.

dijkstra's algorithm.text: An algorithm that finds the shortest paths from a source node to every other node in a weighted graph, such as a road network.

a* search algorithm.text: A graph search algorithm that finds the cheapest path from a start node to a goal node by extending the path with the lowest cost so far plus an estimate of the cost still to go.

geocoding.text: Turning a text description of a location, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates, usually a latitude and longitude pair.

contraction hierarchies.text: A speed-up technique for shortest-path queries that precomputes shortcuts in a road graph so a query can skip unimportant vertices.

map tiles.text: A world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small image blocks that the client joins seamlessly, each requested separately.

web mercator projection.text: A variant of the Mercator map projection that applies spherical formulas to WGS 84 coordinates and is the standard for web mapping.

non-blocking algorithm.text: An algorithm is non-blocking if the failure or suspension of any thread cannot cause the failure or suspension of another thread.

order types.text: The standard instructions a trader can place on a trading venue, such as market, limit and stop orders, each with its own execution rules.

fix protocol.text: An electronic communications protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions and markets.

order book.text: The list of orders that a trading venue, in particular a stock exchange, uses to record the interest of buyers and sellers in a financial instrument.

market data.text: Price and other related data for a financial instrument, reported by a trading venue such as a stock exchange.

matching engine.text: The component that uses the order book to determine which buy and sell orders can be fully or partially executed.

processor affinity.text: Also called CPU pinning, it binds a process or thread to a CPU or a range of CPUs so that it executes only on the designated processors.

collaborative real-time editing.text: Letting several users edit the same document at once on different devices, with their edits merged automatically and nearly instantly.

low-latency critical path design.text: Getting very low latency by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage.

operational transformation.text: A technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits by transforming each operation's parameters against the effects of concurrent operations already executed.

groupware concurrency control.text: Concurrency control for groupware, computer systems that support two or more users working on a common task through a shared environment.

double-entry bookkeeping.text: A bookkeeping method in which every financial transaction is recorded with equal and opposite entries, debits and credits, so the books balance.

payment service provider.text: A third-party company that lets businesses accept electronic payments, such as credit card and debit card payments.

payment settlement systems.text: A payment system is any system used to settle financial transactions through the transfer of monetary value.

payment gateway.text: A merchant service that authorizes credit card or direct payment processing for e-businesses, online retailers and traditional stores.

card payment authorization and settlemen.text: The steps by which a card payment is authorized by the issuing bank, then cleared and settled so the merchant's acquiring bank is funded.

payment reconciliation.text: The process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other.

short message service.text: A mostly paid text messaging service of telephone and mobile systems that lets phones exchange short text messages over cellular networks.

firebase cloud messaging.text: A cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications between app servers and client apps.

apple push notification service.text: Apple's platform notification service that lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices.

access control list.text: A list of permissions attached to a system resource that says which users or system processes may access it and which operations they may perform.

role-based access control.text: An approach to restricting system access to authorized users, defined around roles and privileges rather than around individual users.

discretionary access control.text: A type of access control that restricts access to objects by the identity of subjects or the groups they belong to, where a subject with a permission can pass it on to others.

attribute-based access control.text: An access control paradigm in which a subject's authorization to perform operations is decided by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the requested operation and sometimes the environment.

policy decision and enforcement points.text: An authorization split into points: a policy is retrieved by a Policy Retrieval Point, evaluated at a Policy Decision Point and enforced at a Policy Enforcement Point.

xacml.text: An XML-based standard markup language for specifying access control policies, published by OASIS.

aaa authorization framework.text: An architectural framework for understanding the authorization of Internet resources and services and for deriving requirements for authorization protocols.

mandatory access control.text: A type of access control in which a secured environment, such as an operating system or database, constrains a subject's ability to access or modify an object under a centrally set policy.

relationship-based access control.text: A model evolved from RBAC in which a subject's permission to access a resource is defined by the relationships between subjects and resources.

separation of duties.text: A requirement that two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations, so no one individual can breach security through dual privilege.
